issues.title: October 2026
issues.intro: Recent research highlights the growing market impact of policy uncertainty and structural frictions across asset classes. Studies from central banks examine how monetary-policy risk and derivatives margin calls drive volatility and liquidity strains, offering critical context for current rates and FX positioning.

papers.title: Can Home Visits Re-Engage Chronically Absent Students? Evidence from the LEAP Program
papers.abstract: Beginning in the summer of 2021, the state of Connecticut launched the Learner Engagement and Attendance Program (LEAP) where home visits by school personnel were conducted with students identified as chronically absent from Connecticut’s 15 most disadvantaged school districts. Home visits were designed to connect students and their families directly with teachers to foster strong connections. We use student-level data from 2021–22 through 2023-24 to estimate event studies of the effect of LEAP on student attendance, chronic absenteeism, disciplinary incidents, and student achievement. Utilizing models that address selection into treatment timing over student observable and unobservable attributes, we find that students who received the LEAP intervention experienced approximately a 4 to 5 percentage point increase in attendance rates, a 13 to 15 percentage point decline in chronic absenteeism, and a 3 to 5 percentage point decline in the number of disciplinary incidents. Notably, initial event studies indicated increasing treatment effects over time, but after correcting for selection on unobservables treatment effects appeared constant over time. These effects were broad based, with similar impacts by gender, race and ethnicity, and free or reduced-price lunch status. These attendance and discipline results provide suggest that the LEAP intervention increased student noncognitive skills.
papers.reason: The research evaluates the impact of home visits on student attendance and chronic absenteeism in Connecticut school districts, bearing no relevance to financial markets.

papers.title: Unraveling the Cobweb of Global Imbalances: Drivers, Vulnerabilities and Adjustment Scenarios
papers.abstract: This paper analyses the evolution and drivers of the stock of global imbalances in order to assess associated vulnerabilities and potential adjustment scenarios. These imbalances have recently increased sharply, with a deterioration in the US net international investment position (NIIP) mirrored by NIIP improvements in most other major economies. We decompose these NIIP changes into their proximate drivers for a sample of 28 economies and find that financial factors (including valuation changes and investment income flows) are the primary drivers of global imbalances at both short and long horizons, while trade also plays a significant role (especially at long horizons). Valuation gains on international investment positions have supported economic growth in many countries since 2010, while also increasing their vulnerability to financial market adjustments. To assess the implications and potential risks, we simulate the spillovers through this cobweb of global imbalances from: (i) a sharp dollar depreciation, (ii) a repricing of equity markets, (iii) higher interest rates, and (iv) a halving of trade imbalances. These scenarios highlight the large international spillovers that would be associated with any reduction in global imbalances, the heterogeneous impact of various rebalancing mechanisms on individual countries and the limits of popular proposals for reducing these imbalances. The persistence of global imbalances underscores the importance of building resilience to the large spillovers that can occur through this cobweb of international exposures.
papers.reason: The paper decomposes net international investment positions across 28 economies and simulates financial shocks from dollar depreciation and asset repricing, directly informing FX and cross-border capital flow analysis.

papers.title: Affirmative Action, Faculty Productivity and Caste Interactions: Evidence from Engineering Colleges in India
papers.abstract: Affirmative action programs are often criticized because of concerns that they result in lower worker productivity and efficiency losses. We study the relative productivity of workers benefiting from an aggressive affirmative action policy in a setting where hiring constraints are mandated upon employers and are typically likely to bind. In India, colleges are required to reserve approximately 50 percent of faculty hires for individuals from disadvantaged caste and social class groups. We collect and analyze data from a nationally representative sample of 50 engineering and technology colleges in India, some of which randomly assign students to classrooms. We find that reservation category faculty have lower levels of education, lower professorial ranks and fewer years of experience in academia than general category faculty who are not hired through reservations. Yet, even with lower qualifications, we do not detect meaningful differences in instructional quality between reservation category faculty and general category faculty across a wide range of measures that include course grades, follow-on course grades, standardized test scores, dropout, attendance, graduate school plans, and graduation. In fact, we find that, at least for immediate effects on course grades, students taught by reservation category faculty perform slightly better than students taught by general category faculty. We also estimate “teacher-like-me” effects of reservation category faculty on the relative course performance and longer-term outcomes of reservation category students and cannot reject the hypothesis of null effects. Furthermore, even in the face of potential discrimination and resentment against faculty hiring quotas, general category students perform slightly better in classrooms taught by reservation category faculty than general category faculty. Finally, estimates of differences between reservation category and general category faculty in several measures of research productivity and administrative service are small in magnitude and not statistically different from zero. The findings have implications for the heated debates over affirmative action programs found in many countries around the world and in India which is now the largest country in the world.
papers.reason: The study analyzes the relative productivity of faculty hired under affirmative action quotas in Indian engineering colleges, offering microeconomic evidence with limited direct macroeconomic or market utility.

papers.title: Saving for the Machines
papers.abstract: When machines can perform a growing share of tasks, growth depends on two margins: how the task structure affects the returns to accumulating machines, and how strongly capital accumulation responds to those returns. I argue that, in a standard task model, capital supply governs the size of the growth boom associated with automation, while the task structure sets the duration of this growth boom and the evolution of wages. I document how the same technology path that generates 11.7% annual growth when households choose their saving rate optimally delivers only 2.2% when the saving rate is fixed at the calibrated U.S. 2025 level of 23%. Therefore, slow growth might reflect too little capital accumulation instead of a technological bottleneck. Also, the saving rate rises mainly because automation raises the capital share, not because households become thriftier. Long yields price the growth boom: the ten-year real yield jumps from 5.1% to 13.6% on impact. In my benchmark calibration, hand-to-mouth households lose the equivalent of two-fifths to two-thirds of their consumption, while keeping them on trend temporarily costs at most a fifth of GDP.
papers.reason: The paper links automation, capital supply, and saving rates to long-run economic growth and demonstrates a sharp impact on ten-year real yields, making it highly relevant for rates and macro strategists.

papers.title: Income Inequality and Intergenerational Mobility in Russia: Trends, Sources, and Measurement
papers.abstract: This chapter documents trends in income and inequality in Russia from the collapse of the Soviet Union through 2025, drawing on official statistics, the existing literature, and household survey microdata. It also reviews evidence on intergenerational mobility. While there is a consensus that inequality dramatically increased during the 1990s, its post-2000 trajectory is contested. Initial household survey studies usually found a decline, whereas official statistics reported a comparatively stable Gini coefficient. Our analysis of Russia's major household surveys, harmonized using common measurement conventions, aligns with the survey-based literature, indicating that the Gini coefficient generally fell from approximately 0.45–0.48 in the early 2000s to 0.29–0.38 in the early 2020s. We further find that most inequality arises within rather than between regions, urban and rural areas, and education and occupation groups. Household labor-market attachment, region, and household composition account for the largest shares of the explained variance in log income. The large literature on inequality is complemented by a small literature on intergenerational mobility. Here, the various studies on intergenerational dynamics in education, occupation, and income across post-Soviet cohorts conclude that, even against the background of dramatic structural changes, family background remains strongly associated with children’s outcomes.
papers.reason: The paper details historical income inequality and intergenerational mobility trends in Russia up to 2025, offering useful micro-data for country-specific sovereign credit and economic risk assessments.

papers.title: Public R&D and the Automation of Manufacturing: Evidence from the Space Race
papers.abstract: This paper examines how public research and development shaped the direction of technological change during the Cold War–era Space Race and its consequences for US manufacturing. While prior research has documented the effects of public R&D on innovation and economic growth, less is known about whether mission-oriented public investment directed innovation toward automation and how this affected labor markets. We exploit variation in exposure to NASA's Space Race investments across industries and locations to estimate the effects of public R&D on innovation and manufacturing outcomes from 1947 to 1992. Combining newly developed measures of automation in full-text patent data with historical evidence on government involvement in patenting, we show that NASA-sponsored patents are systematically more automation-intensive than non-NASA patents within the same technological classes. Industries and locations more exposed to Space Race activity experienced persistent declines in labor share, consistent with the diffusion of labor-saving technologies developed for space applications. In contrast, we find little evidence of systematic changes in skill composition. These findings show that mission-oriented public R&D can shape the direction of technological change and have lasting distributional consequences.
papers.reason: By examining how public R&D directed toward automation impacted US manufacturing labor shares from 1947 to 1992, the study offers structural context for long-term labor market and productivity trends.

papers.title: Aggregate-Surplus Maximizing Monetary Policy
papers.abstract: We study optimal monetary policy in a general heterogeneous-agent New Keynesian (HANK) economy. Instead of maximizing a social welfare function, the policymaker maximizes the joint surplus of all households, without taking a stance on how that surplus should be distributed. This is the policy that maximizes resources left over if winners from reform were to compensate losers. We derive the approximate optimal policy using linear-quadratic methods. The quadratic objective function nests the standard New Keynesian loss function and adds losses from incomplete markets and heterogeneous labor wedges. We show that optimal policy is the sum of time-dependent and state-contingent components. When labor wedges are homogeneous, monetary policy cannot improve household insurance: the time-dependent component is zero, and optimal policy coincides with the representative-agent New Keynesian (RANK) benchmark. Departures from RANK arise from heterogeneous labor wedges. In that case, the time-dependent component temporarily alleviates incomplete-market distortions but vanishes over time. The state-contingent component solves a dual-mandate problem, as in RANK, but with a higher weight on output-gap stabilization relative to inflation stabilization. In a calibrated model, heterogeneous labor wedges raise this weight by about 37 percent. We also find that a dual mandate with this higher weight achieves almost all of the aggregate-surplus gains from the full optimal policy and requires no compensatory transfers between winners and losers.
papers.reason: The paper provides theoretical insights into optimal monetary policy using a HANK framework, altering optimal weights on output gaps versus inflation, which directly informs central bank reaction function analysis.

papers.title: The Effects of Monetary Policy on Macroeconomic Expectations: High-Frequency Evidence from Prediction Markets
papers.abstract: When the Federal Reserve raises interest rates, standard macroeconomic models and VARs predict that output, employment, and inflation should fall over the next several quarters. However, monthly-frequency professional macroeconomic forecast revisions are sometimes positively correlated with Fed interest rate changes, leading to a debate about what could explain these puzzling correlations. We bring to bear new high-frequency data on this question from macroeconomic event contracts traded on Kalshi, a CFTC-licensed, U.S.-based event trading exchange and prediction market. These high-frequency event contracts allow us to isolate and estimate the effects of monetary policy and other announcements on Kalshi market-implied macroeconomic expectations. Our results are consistent with standard transmission channels from monetary policy to the macroeconomy, with little or no role for a “Fed Information Effect”.
papers.reason: Uses high-frequency prediction market data to isolate monetary policy transmission and discount the Fed Information Effect, offering timely insights for rates and macro strategists.

papers.title: Pollution Monitoring and the Pricing of Environmental Risk in Firms
papers.abstract: Pricing firms’ environmental risk is central to ensuring that capital is efficiently allocated. We examine whether an increase in the salience of pollution information affects the beliefs and perceived valuations of financially sophisticated agents—financial analysts—regarding the environmental risks faced by the firms they cover. Exploiting the staggered rollout of China's ambient air quality monitoring program, we show that when monitoring is introduced in a city, analysts based there become substantially more likely to discuss air pollution. These changes in attention are reflected in stock prices: reports issued by treated analysts generate more negative market reactions for brown firms and more positive reactions for green firms, with little change for environmentally neutral firms. These price responses do not subsequently reverse. Treated analysts increase their information acquisition through corporate site visits and issue less favorable assessments of brown firms and more favorable assessments of green firms. Our findings show that ambient environmental monitoring can affect asset prices by making environmental risks more salient and inducing greater information production about their implications for firm value.
papers.reason: Shows that pollution monitoring in China affects analyst attention and corporate asset prices, providing direct evidence on how environmental risk is priced in emerging equities.

papers.title: A Beckerian Theory of Taxation
papers.abstract: We study taxation in matching environments in which both equilibrium sorting and the sharing of match surplus are endogenous. Tax reforms lead to complex adjustments in sorting and surplus sharing patterns across the whole economy. We develop a general approach for characterizing these equilibrium adjustments using matching elasticities, which are primitive objects that describe how agents' matching choices are affected by pecuniary payoffs in partial equilibrium. Applying this approach to a workhorse model of family formation, we first show that the sorting and surplus sharing responses are closely linked to complementarities in the creation of economic surplus, as first emphasized by Becker (1973). We then describe the effects of arbitrary tax reforms on tax revenues, the utilities of different agents, and social welfare; design tests to assess Pareto efficiency of existing tax systems; derive formulas that characterize optimal taxes; and propose numerical techniques to compute them. In a calibrated model, we find that optimal marginal tax rates are substantially lower and less progressive than in the Mirrleesian benchmark.
papers.reason: Develops a theoretical framework for taxation in matching models with endogenous sorting, offering primarily academic contributions to optimal tax theory.

papers.title: Coase Meets Negishi: Property Rights, Welfare Weights, and Distributional Consequences in Climate Economics
papers.abstract: We develop a property-rights based approach for defining welfare weights in economic models of climate change. Whether there is a "right to pollute" or a "right to no pollution" is increasingly contested in legislatures, courts, and international climate negotiations. We show how these notions of property rights can provide the basis for "Coasean welfare weights" that are applicable in multilateral public goods settings. Distributional questions are addressed through positive analysis, conditional on property rights, rather than normative views about redistribution. The implied transfers are consistent with a bargained solution over the net benefits of addressing climate change and reflect the value of property rights over emissions. The approach defines efficient allocations that generate Pareto improvements, in contrast to commonly used Negishi weights. We implement the approach in a global integrated assessment model to quantify what countries have at stake in ongoing political and legal debates about emissions-related property rights.
papers.reason: Introduces property-rights-based welfare weights for climate models, providing useful conceptual framing for long-term ESG and climate policy analysis.

papers.title: Governance Regimes, Economic Mobility, and the Composition of Public Investment: Evidence from the Democratization of Villages in India
papers.abstract: We develop a quantifiable general-equilibrium model of village governance, motivated by India’s democratization, to study how political institutions shape public goods provision and economic development. The model features two groups, landowners and landless workers, with different preferences over public goods such as irrigation, schools, and employment programs. Households from both groups can enter nonfarm entrepreneurship, but face credit-dependent entry costs. We compare oligarchy, where landowners control public goods decisions, with democracy, where electoral competition determines policy based on the relative sizes of the two groups. The calibrated model predicts that democratization’s effects on public goods and growth are not uniform; they depend on population composition and the ease of occupational mobility through access to credit. Using a 37-year village-level panel from India (1971–2006) and exploiting variation in democratization driven by state and national reforms, we find strong support for these predictions. Financial intermediation shifts landless households’ preferences from wage-enhancing policies toward schooling, increasing nonfarm business entry. As a result, democracy provides fewer schools than oligarchy when credit is unavailable, but more schools when credit is accessible. We also show that transfers to the landless increase schooling under democracy but reduce it under oligarchy. These findings highlight how governance structures and economic conditions jointly determine the effectiveness of development policies.
papers.reason: Analyzes how democratization and credit access shape public goods provision and entrepreneurship in rural India, offering micro-level insights with indirect macro relevance.

papers.title: Risk and Return in Government Bonds
papers.abstract: Does the compensation investors require for holding government bonds vary with their risk? We measure expected excess returns using market yields and professional forecasts of future yields, showing that they are tightly linked to a standard measure of risk: bonds’ betas with respect to the stock market. In a month-by-maturity panel of U. S. Treasuries from 1988 to 2024, the correlation between expected excess returns and bond–stock betas is 67%. The correlation is driven by variation in market yields rather than forecasters’ expectations. The relationship between realized excess returns and betas is weak in a univariate regression, but it becomes economically large and significant when we control for monetary-policy and macroeconomic forecast errors. Similar results obtain in an international panel of developed countries from 1989 to 2024. Our findings suggest that variation in risk premia driven by changing bond risk accounts for more than half of both the decline in U.S. long-term bond yields since the mid-1980s and their increase since 2020.
papers.reason: Links bond-stock betas to expected excess returns in US Treasuries and international developed markets, explaining historical yield movements and directly informing fixed income strategy.

papers.title: How Different are Different Differences-in-Differences? A Large-Scale Meta-Analysis
papers.abstract: I use AI-assisted replication to assess the empirical importance of negative weights in two-way fixed effects (TWFE) estimation, drawing on 1,346 staggered-adoption specifications from 108 economics papers. TWFE estimates are highly correlated with estimates from modern difference-in-differences methods, with observed sign reversals in 10.8–14.5% of comparisons and greater precision for TWFE. Hierarchical models that account for estimation noise imply a 91–98% correlation between estimands and a 0.6–2.1% probability of obtaining a statistically significant TWFE estimate with the opposite sign from the modern estimand. These findings suggest negative weights may be a less serious problem in practice, and illustrate how AI can support large-scale empirical assessments of new econometric methods.
papers.reason: Evaluates difference-in-differences estimators using AI, representing pure methodological research without direct market or macro applications.

papers.title: The Global Office: How Globalisation’s Frontier is Shifting from Factories to Offices
papers.abstract: This paper argues that globalisation’s frontier has shifted from manufacturing GVCs to services GVCs: from the Global Factory to the Global Office. While the Factory remains larger in gross trade, the Office is growing much faster. A heatmap of trade in intermediates shows that the Factory is bloc-shaped and dominated by China, whereas the Office is star-shaped and dominated by America. Gravity estimates show that distance matters less for Office exports, but time zones matter more: each hour of time-zone separation reduces Office exports by roughly 4%, while having no effect on Factory exports. Importantly, all of the world’s export-linked net job creation between 2008 and 2022 occurred in digitally delivered services rather than manufacturing, and trade-linked service jobs command higher average pay globally. The Factory-to-Office shift is also reshaping development. Most emerging economies have seen export-led growth tilt towards services, but their service exports are not yet large enough to drive overall GDP growth the way manufacturing did historically. The big picture is that globalisation’s second unbundling is running out of steam even as its third unbundling is powering ahead. The paper, which raises more questions than it answers, closes with the conjecture that the future of trade is services.
papers.reason: Examines the structural shift from manufacturing to digitally delivered services in global trade, offering useful context for long-term global growth and labor dynamics.

papers.title: Manufacturing Renaissance Meets Time-Inconsistent Tariffs
papers.abstract: We analyze optimal tariffs in a dynamic version of the Venables (1987) framework with a time-to-build lag in firm creation. In this environment, trade protection is driven by the desire to increase firm creation at home at the expense of the foreign trade partner. When firm creation takes time, the benefits of protection accrue in the future, whereas the costs in the form of higher consumer prices occur immediately. Under certain parameterizations, a policymaker that can commit to a full time path of tariffs leaves trade unrestricted at date 0, and announces high tariffs coming on at a pre-specified future period. But there is a time inconsistency: the policymaker's short-run incentive is not to impose contemporaneous tariffs due to the adverse effect on prices. Thus, lack of commitment to future tariffs can preserve free(er) trade and derail a manufacturing renaissance.
papers.reason: The theoretical analysis of time-inconsistent tariffs and manufacturing promotion sheds light on trade policy dynamics and protectionism risks.

papers.title: Fixed/Floating Interest Rate Parity
papers.abstract: We present a new no-arbitrage relation which we denote as fixed/floating interest rate parity. This relation can be viewed as a domestic version of covered interest rate parity. We test this relation using fixed-rate bonds and floating-rate notes in the multi-trillion U.S. agency debt market and document significant violations. These violations are largely unrelated to other arbitrage spreads and measures of intermediary constraints. Instead, they are closely tied to the behavior of money market funds which hold the vast majority of agency floating-rate notes. Our results identify clientele effects as a source of persistent mispricing.
papers.reason: Documenting significant arbitrage violations in the US agency debt market via fixed/floating interest rate parity, the paper provides actionable insights for rates and fixed income trading desks.

papers.title: Coordinated R&D Programs and the Creation of New Industries
papers.abstract: Large, mission-oriented R&D efforts sometimes generate substantial technological advances, but their commercial impacts vary. This paper uses one such effort—the U.S. World War II radar program—to explore how the outputs of such programs may contribute to later commercial development. Using archival records together with data on firm entry, patenting, and technical labor flows, we reconstruct the organization and outputs of wartime radar R&D, document the rapid postwar growth of a civilian industry, and evaluate which outputs were used in subsequent commercial activity. Codified knowledge (in publications and patents) diffused broadly, embodied knowledge (trained personnel) diffused more locally, and the component-system industrial architecture of the wartime program was mirrored in firms' postwar commercial positions. The evidence points to specific channels through which coordinated technology development programs can give shape to emerging high-tech industries.
papers.reason: The historical analysis of WWII US radar programs and commercial industry creation offers indirect perspectives on the long-term structural effects of coordinated R&D and industrial policy.

papers.title: What Drives Censorship on College Campuses?
papers.abstract: There has been widespread concern about self-censorship on university campuses, and especially that conservative voices are being stifled. Using survey data from a private elite college, we show that self-censorship is not simply about being conservative: it is students with the most moderate views who self-censor the most. This pattern is associated with confidence and salience — students who are more confident in their views or who see an issue as especially important tend to hold more extreme views and to self-censor less. At the same time, conservatives self-censor at higher rates than liberals, and the same individual is more likely to self-censor on the views where they are relatively more conservative than on those where they are relatively more liberal; conservatives are also far more likely than liberals to cite concerns about social exclusion as a reason for self-censoring, and report self-censoring less outside the university community. Groups perceived as marginalized self-censor less than majority groups, and especially so on issues salient to them (e.g., Black students on BLM).
papers.reason: The research focuses on the micro-level drivers of self-censorship among college students at a private elite college, with no implications for macroeconomic or financial analysis.

papers.title: Demand-Driven Inflation
papers.abstract: Post-covid inflation was predominantly driven by unexpectedly strong demand forces---both in the United States and in the Euro Area. We establish this result using a sequence of structural VARs with progressively richer specifications, interpret it through the lens of standard AD-AS analysis and an estimated DSGE model, and provide independent support for this conclusion using survey forecasts and real-time data. These demand forces reflected a combination of surprisingly robust pent-up demand following the pandemic restrictions, stronger-than-expected expansionary fiscal policies, and an unusually accommodative monetary stance. Together, they mitigated the recessionary effects of adverse supply shocks and supported the recovery, albeit at the cost of higher inflation. The economic intuition is simple: When a central bank responds forcefully to inflationary pressures, as the Fed and the ECB have done in recent decades, the aggregate demand curve is relatively flat, so supply disturbances move real activity much more than inflation. A large inflation surge, therefore, requires a shift or rotation of the aggregate demand curve.
papers.reason: Using structural VARs and DSGE models for the US and Euro Area, the paper demonstrates that post-covid inflation was primarily driven by demand forces, directly informing monetary policy and inflation outlooks.

papers.title: Beyond the Numbers: Professional Forecasters’ Narratives about Inflation and Stock Market Performance
papers.abstract: Professional forecasters' heterogeneous narratives about how inflation affects stock markets in 2023 rationalize their high disagreement regarding quantitative expectations for 12-month-ahead inflation and stock returns in December 2022. Professional forecasters causally update their return expectations in heterogeneous directions in response to information about the inflation outlook, depending on the narrative they entertain. Moreover, the narratives also affect their asset allocation in a hypothetical portfolio-choice experiment. Providing common signals does not necessarily lead to convergence of beliefs if agents subscribe to different narratives.
papers.reason: The paper investigates how professional forecasters' narratives regarding inflation and stock markets drive disagreement in expectations and portfolio choices, offering useful context for sentiment analysis.

papers.title: Green Tastes, Beliefs, and Portfolios: Evidence from Synthetic Investors
papers.abstract: We use LLMs as synthetic survey respondents to elicit green tastes, return beliefs, portfolio allocations, and investment motives from 480 retail and 60 institutional investor identities. Compared with retail, institutions report weaker tastes yet greener portfolio tilts, citing outside pressure. A greener tilt therefore need not indicate a stronger taste for greenness. Retail tastes depend mostly on political affiliation, institutional tastes on type and geography. Beliefs differ across the three ESG dimensions, with high-governance portfolios expected to outperform. We reconstruct survey responses under 2014--2025 information environments using date-masked information modules shuffled across years. Tastes vary little over time, but beliefs about green portfolios become more pessimistic after 2020. The two reconstructed series relate to different real-world data: tastes to measures of green demand, beliefs to measures of attention.
papers.reason: The study uses synthetic investor identities to analyze ESG portfolio tilts, tastes, and beliefs, providing indirect insights for sustainable finance and equity asset management.

papers.title: Universities as Incubators of Mass Uprising
papers.abstract: We link high-frequency geocoded protest data during Bangladesh’s 2024 Monsoon Revolution, Facebook measures of protest activity and social connectivity, university enrollment and demographics to establish: (1) student-linked protests precede off-campus mobilization; (2) student concentration predicts both on- and off-campus protest, while non-student youth, educated adults, urbanization, and locations of “placebo” universities authorized but not yet operating do not; and (3) social connectivity to student protest locations predicts off-campus diffusion one week later. Universities appear to incubate mass uprising by making dissent visible, coordinated, and capable of spreading beyond campus. Such patterns are also evident in U.S. Vietnam War protests and in global data. That universities facilitate broader political mobilization can explain why governments often seek to restrict student activism.
papers.reason: The paper examines the dynamics of student protests and political mobilization in Bangladesh and globally, offering little direct relevance for financial markets or macroeconomic forecasting.

papers.title: News shocks and inflation: theory and evidence from large oil discoveries
papers.abstract: We study how news shocks affect inflation in open economies, using large oil and gas discoveries with realized production lags of at least five years as observable news about future output. Panel local projections show that discoveries raise core consumer prices over the subsequent decade, with about half the increase occurring prior to extraction.
papers.reason: Using large oil discoveries as identified news shocks, the paper demonstrates that anticipated supply increases affect core inflation well before extraction.

papers.title: Bank liquidity regulation and the growth of private credit
papers.abstract: We study the role of bank liquidity regulation in the growth of private credit. Following the introduction of the liquidity coverage ratio (LCR), private credit increases significantly more in U.S. counties with a larger footprint of banks subject to the LCR or of LCR banks with greater initial liquidity shortfalls.
papers.reason: Investigates the impact of the liquidity coverage ratio on private credit growth using US data, directly informing banking stability and credit market dynamics.

papers.title: Inflation after the Iran war
papers.abstract: An unexpected increase in energy costs raises inflation directly through flexibly-set prices. Whether that shock amplifies to a larger and persistent rise in inflation depends on its transmission through the economy.
papers.reason: The abstract is incomplete and lacks details, but addresses the transmission of energy cost shocks to persistent inflation.

papers.title: Competing rails for crossborder payments: banks, fintechs, and stablecoins
papers.abstract: Competing rails for crossborder payments: banks, fintechs, and stablecoins We focus on the costs of cross-border payments across three payment channels: traditional banks, fintech money transfer operators (MTOs) and stablecoin-based transfers. Despite improvements in domestic payment systems, sending money internationally remains expensive, particularly for small transfers. We examine how payment architecture, foreign exchange (FX) pricing and intermediary fees shape these costs. It also studies whether stablecoins can overcome the frictions associated with existing payment channels. Combining intraday pricing from fintech MTOs, World Bank remittance data, bank wire transactions and crypto market data, we construct comparable measures of cross-border payment costs across currencies and transfer sizes. We distinguish FX markups from explicit fees, including exchange trading charges, blockchain transaction fees and fiat withdrawal costs. We examine both transfers using a single dollar-linked stablecoin and those involving on-chain exchanges between stablecoins denominated in different currencies. There are three sets of findings. First, fintech money transfer operators (MTOs) substantially reduce cross-border payment costs relative to traditional retail bank wires. In our small sample of bank transactions, FX markups range from approximately 2 to 4.7%, even for highly liquid currencies and before accounting for explicit wire fees.
papers.reason: The paper compares costs, FX markups, and explicit fees across traditional banks, fintechs, and stablecoins, providing direct relevance for FX and payment market structures.

papers.title: Geoeconomic pressure
papers.abstract: Geoeconomic pressure-the use of existing economic relationships by governments to achieve geopolitical or economic goals-is a prominent feature of global power dynamics.This paper introduces a methodology using large language models (LLMs) to systematically identify the application of and response to geoeconomic pressure from large textual corpora.We classify which governments apply pressure to which foreign targets, using which instruments, firms, and products.We demonstrate that firms affected by tariffs respond primarily with price changes whereas firms affected by export controls respond disproportionately by investing in research and development.We document significant heterogeneity in how firms respond to pressure based on whether their home government is applying the pressure, whether their home country is the recipient of the pressure, or whether they are based in an affected third party country.Finally, we quantify the degree of measurement uncertainty generated by the LLM-based analysis by comparing the classifications across multiple open-weight models as well as considering a wide range of variations of our prompts.
papers.reason: The paper provides a methodological framework to track firm-level responses to tariffs and export controls, relevant for supply chain and trade analysis.

papers.title: Offshore forwards and exchange rate transmission in emerging markets
papers.abstract: We study how offshore non-deliverable forward (NDF) markets transmit exchange-rate pressures to domestic currency markets. Using unique transaction-level data on the universe of centrally cleared NDFs for ten emerging-market currencies over 2013–2025, we show that offshore NDF order flow moves both offshore forward and domestic spot exchange rates and widens the offshore–onshore forward spread.
papers.reason: Uses transaction-level data across ten emerging-market currencies to demonstrate how offshore NDF order flow transmits exchange-rate pressures and affects domestic spot markets.

analysis.summary: This paper examines how trading activity in offshore non-deliverable forward (NDF) markets transmits exchange-rate pressure to domestic currency markets in emerging economies. Utilizing transaction-level clearing data for ten emerging-market currencies from 2013 to 2025, the authors demonstrate that offshore order flow moves both offshore forward and domestic spot exchange rates while widening the offshore-onshore forward spread. The transmission occurs primarily because dealers holding NDF positions hedge their inventory risk directly in domestic spot markets. Consequently, capital controls and dealer balance-sheet constraints dictate the extent to which offshore speculative demand drives onshore exchange-rate volatility.
key_takeaways: A $1 billion long-USD NDF order flow depreciates domestic spot rates by ~10 basis points and offshore NDF rates by ~18 basis points across 10 EM currencies (2013–2025).
Spot price impact is state-dependent, dropping from 17.8 basis points when dealer gross FX positions are one standard deviation below mean to 7.1 basis points when above.
Offshore order flow transmits to domestic spot rates via dealer hedging, while balance-sheet costs and capital controls determine the magnitude of the offshore–onshore spread.
analysis.relevance: This research provides actionable insights for EM FX strategists, risk managers, and macro investors tracking foreign exchange microstructure under capital controls. By establishing how offshore NDF order flow affects domestic spot markets across ten major EM currencies, the study equips research teams to model currency spillovers and cross-market spreads. Strategists can apply these metrics to evaluate dealer balance-sheet capacity, anticipate spot volatility, and assess regulatory changes governing domestic bank access to offshore NDF trading.
analysis.market_focus_rationale: The study focuses exclusively on price discovery, capital controls, and exchange-rate dynamics across ten emerging-market currencies.

papers.title: Are stablecoins and bank deposits substitutes?
papers.abstract: We test whether stablecoins and bank deposits act as substitutes by estimating the semi-elasticity of stablecoin market capitalization with respect to deposit rate changes. Using local projections fit to weekly U.S. data from January 2019 to June 2025, we find that deposit rate increases predict slower stablecoin growth. To address endogeneity, we exploit a nonlinearity in deposit rate pass-through.
papers.reason: It addresses banking sector liquidity and monetary transmission by empirically testing whether stablecoins substitute for bank deposits using U.S. data.

papers.title: Transformative AI and demand bottlenecks
papers.abstract: Transformative AI promises to accelerate growth through productivity enhancement and automation. Yet automation on such a scale would raise the share of investment in output, potentially starving AI innovation of returns from a shrinking consumer market.
papers.reason: Explores the macroeconomic and demand-side bottlenecks of transformative AI and automation, offering conceptual background for long-term growth and productivity outlooks.

papers.title: Chasing El Dorado: gold under shifting geopolitical and financial conditions
papers.abstract: This paper analyses the state-dependent effects of geopolitical risks on gold prices (i.e. the safe-haven role of gold), conditional on financial conditions. Geopolitical risks are often associated with tighter financial conditions. However, recent data reveal a decoupling between such shocks and more restrictive financial conditions, raising the question of how gold returns are affected by geopolitical shocks, conditional on the macro-financial environment.
papers.reason: Examining state-dependent gold returns under shifting geopolitical and financial conditions informs safe-haven asset allocation and FX strategy.

papers.title: Maritime chokepoints and the global economy: evidence from the Strait of Hormuz
papers.abstract: The conflict in the Middle East and the subsequent disruption of traffic in the Strait of Hormuz have triggered an unprecedented shock to the global economy. Using historical data from the IMF/University of Oxford Portwatch database on maritime traffic, this paper empirically examines some of the potential economic and financial consequences of disruptions to traffic in the Strait of Hormuz.
papers.reason: Examines the macro-financial consequences of maritime disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, offering clear relevance for inflation and energy market risks.

papers.title: Hidden by complexity? Measuring stablecoin, crypto and decentralised finance ecosystems
papers.abstract: Decentralised finance data presents a distinctive paradox: while every data point is publicly recorded and accessible, deriving meaningful insights is obscured by the scale, fragmentation and complexity of the ecosystem. Key metrics illustrate that the rapidly evolving DeFi ecosystem introduces unique challenges for economic and financial research in accurately capturing financial activity in DeFi.
papers.reason: Discusses the measurement challenges and structural complexity of decentralised finance ecosystems, with indirect relevance to digital asset tracking.

papers.title: What determines banks' excess demand for reserves?
papers.abstract: What determines banks' excess demand for reserves? The amount of central bank reserves to supply has become a highly contentious policy issue for many central banks that shrink their balance sheets which were built up during quantitative easing. However, there is little evidence about the amount of reserves banks actually want to hold and the factors that shape this choice. To trace bank-level demand for reserves empirically, we exploit new microdata and a unique feature of Sveriges Riksbank's operational framework, under which banks reveal their demand for excess reserves every week. We examine the factors that drive their choice to hold excess reserves, ie to keep reserves at the central bank rather than invest them in other instruments that provide higher returns. Most existing work estimates reserve demand for the banking system as a whole. Bank-level data on reserve holdings and money market trading are rarely available, and central banks tend to adjust the supply of reserves in response to the very forces that shape demand. Our setting avoids both problems: supply is fully elastic, and banks reveal their own demand for excess reserves week by week. Ours is the first study of bank-level factors that shape the demand for reserves, and contributes to the broader policy debate about the size of central bank balance sheets and "demand-driven floors". Banks hold substantial excess reserves even though doing so is costly.
papers.reason: Utilizes unique microdata to analyze bank-level excess demand for reserves, offering direct insights for central bank balance sheet reduction and liquidity management.

papers.title: Zombie firms in emerging Asia: domestic and cross border implications
papers.abstract: Zombie firms in emerging Asia: domestic and cross border implications This paper analyses the macroeconomic implications of zombie firms in Asian emerging market economies (EMEs) in both the domestic and cross-border contexts. We use firm-bank linked data for 10 EMEs over 2005–21. To identify the cross-border spillover channels of Asian EME zombie firms for inflation and growth in advanced economies (AEs), we consider both the trade-weighted and cross-border lending-weighted exposures of the AEs to the Asian EME zombie firms. We provide the first evidence that zombie-induced disinflation transmits across borders through global value chain (GVC) linkages, by identifying zombie prevalence in GVC-connected economies. We also conduct a direct horse race between the trade and bank lending channels of international zombie transmission. In addition, we provide micro-level evidence on the asymmetric behaviour of domestic versus foreign banks in evergreening analysis in the domestic and cross-border contexts. Finally, we fill a gap in the zombie firm literature, which has mostly looked at AEs, by focusing on Asian EMEs central to GVCs. First, we find that the number of zombie firms in Asian EMEs has increased significantly over 2005-21, sustained by evergreening by weak banks. Second, zombie prevalence domestically depresses firm performance, crowds out healthy firms and lowers inflation and GDP growth.
papers.reason: Provides firm-bank linked evidence from Asian emerging markets on how zombie firms and bank evergreening depress domestic growth and transmit disinflation internationally through GVCs.

papers.title: Verifiable official statistics: a blockchain-based approach
papers.abstract: International organisations including the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) have adopted SDMx (Statistical Data and Metadata) as the standard for exchanging official statistics. Trust in published data is essential for evidence-based policymaking. This paper shows how binding each SDMx dataset to its source using blockchain technology can enhance confidence in official statistics.
papers.reason: Discusses a technical application of blockchain to official statistics standards, with negligible direct impact on financial market pricing or macro analysis.

papers.title: Settlement liquidity in the Colombian large-value payment system: the role of reserve requirements
papers.abstract: This paper analyzes the intraday timing of transactions in Colombia's large-value payment system (CUD) from 2018 to 2025, focusing on how changes in reserve requirements affect liquidity management by financial institutions. Using high-frequency transaction data, we document that reductions in reserve requirements in April 2020 and September 2024 are associated with a shift of settlement activity toward later hours of the day.
papers.reason: Analyzes how reserve requirement changes impact intraday settlement timing in Colombia's large-value payment system, informing liquidity management and funding conditions.

papers.title: Hard to shift, easy to reshape: central bank reserve demand and frictions
papers.abstract: How far can central banks shrink their balance sheets? The answer sets the limits to quantitative tightening (QT), and depends critically on the demand for reserves and whether the drivers widely thought to have increased it over the past decade actually do so. We assess the impact of three such drivers: post-crisis liquidity regulation, monetization frictions, and fragmented interbank markets.
papers.reason: Directly addresses the limits of central bank balance sheet reduction and reserve demand drivers, crucial for rates and liquidity strategy.

papers.title: What drives exchange rate pass-throughs? Evidence from a non-parametric method
papers.abstract: We provide new evidence on the drivers of the pass-through of exchange rate movements into consumer prices across four decades and close to a hundred countries, combining econometrics and random forests.
papers.reason: Combines non-parametric methods and econometrics across close to a hundred countries over four decades to document drivers of exchange rate pass-through to consumer prices.

papers.title: Dollarisation and monetary control: what lessons for the rise of stablecoins?
papers.abstract: We document that historical deposit dollarisation and recent stablecoin flows are both associated with similar macro-financial drivers, including the strength of exchange rate pass-through and sovereign or banking crises.
papers.reason: Links historical deposit dollarisation and recent stablecoin flows to common macro-financial drivers, offering direct insights for monetary control and digital asset adoption.

papers.title: The evolving nexus: sovereigns, banks and NBFIs
papers.abstract: The evolving nexus: sovereigns, banks and NBFIs Historically, banks' holdings of sovereign debt have been key drivers of the co-movement between sovereign and bank risks. Recent years have seen an increase in banks' links with non-bank financial institutions (NBFIs) as well as a greater presence of NBFIs in sovereign debt markets. These developments have the potential to broaden the classical sovereign-bank nexus into a sovereign-bank-NBFI nexus. We examine the degree to which this has taken place, using European bank-level data along with global country-level data. Our paper is the first to formally analyse whether there has been a fundamental change in the way sovereign risk is transmitted to the financial system. More concretely, we examine the degrees to which the co-movement between sovereign and bank risk is driven by banks' exposures to sovereigns and NBFIs. This has important implications for the analysis of the key risks facing the global financial system and for the policies needed to address them. We find that banks' direct sovereign exposures have recently become less important in explaining the co-movement between bank and sovereign risk. By contrast, banks' exposures to NBFIs have become a significant determinant of the bank-sovereign risk co-movement. We also find evidence that NBFIs' sovereign debt holdings have become important drivers of the co-movement between NBFI and sovereign risk.
papers.reason: The study provides empirical evidence that bank exposures to NBFIs have replaced direct sovereign exposures as key drivers of risk co-movement, directly informing sovereign and financial stability assessments.

papers.title: Geopolitical risk and emerging market sovereign risk premia
papers.abstract: This study examines the determinants of sovereign risk, focusing on the impact of geopolitical risk in emerging market economies (EMEs) sovereign risk metrics. Using local projection techniques, we evaluate the effects of geopolitical risk on credit default swaps (CDS) and EMBI indices in EMEs, including the recent war between Ukraine and Russia. Our findings highlight the significance of considering geopolitical risk when analyzing risk premiums for emerging markets. Notably, we find that the impact of geopolitical risk shocks on CDS is higher than the effect on EMBI spread dynamics. Furthermore, using recursive estimations, we show that the effect of geopolitical risk on sovereign CDS and EMBI spreads has been relatively stable. On the other hand, we find an important degree of heterogeneity across countries by analyzing evidence from individual countries. Some countries in our sample seem statistically unaffected by geopolitical risk, particularly when examining EMBI dynamics.
papers.reason: Evaluates the impact of geopolitical risk shocks on emerging market CDS and EMBI spreads using local projections, providing direct inputs for EM sovereign credit analysis.

papers.title: The AI investment race
papers.abstract: Exuberance about new technologies often brings about investment booms. The race among firms to capture a share of the revenues can result in excessive investment that makes the boom prone to a disruptive end. The boom-bust cycle recurs across history, from the canal and railway manias of the 19th century to the dotcom boom of the 1990s. The current artificial intelligence (AI) build-out ranks among the largest technology-driven investment booms in US history. Could it share the same fate as prior episodes? We model the AI boom as a race between firms in a winner-take-most environment. Contest externalities induce firms to over-commit capital relative to the social returns from the technology. The use of debt and circular stakes to finance investment introduces financial fragility, exposing firms to fire sales of specialised assets in busts. We calibrate the model using data from company accounts and disclosed deals to obtain quantitative insights. Finally, we analyse the risk of systemic contagion arising from circular financial linkages within the sector. The AI race generates significant over-investment, exceeding the socially efficient level by around 50% under a conservative baseline. Larger booms end in more disruptive busts. As AI hardware is specialised, fire- sale dynamics induce losses that grow with debt. The rush to commit investment early to gain a head start also increases vulnerability and raises the likelihood of a bust.
papers.reason: Using US company data and a structural model, the paper quantifies over-investment risks and financial fragility in the artificial intelligence build-out, relevant for equity and credit strategists.

papers.title: Assessing the effects of recent provisioning rules on consumer credit allocation in Colombia
papers.abstract: In January 2023, Colombia introduced new banking rules. These rules required banks to set aside more money to cover risks from long-term consumer loans. This paper looks at how these changes affected banks and their lending practices.
papers.reason: Investigates the impact of new banking provisioning rules on consumer credit allocation in Colombia, directly relevant for banking stability and credit conditions in the region.

papers.title: Financial and real effects of fiscal risk
papers.abstract: terms. We find that fiscal risk shocks, on average, lead to higher borrowing costs, currency depreciation and lower equity valuations. Prices of goods and services also rise on impact and stay elevated for about one year, with inflation expectations moving alongside them. Output enjoys a temporary boost, but this dissipates quickly and is followed by a persistent contraction induced by tighter financial conditions. The effects of fiscal risk intensify when central banks keep policy accommodative and allow real interest rates to remain negative. The effects are also more pronounced when sovereign risk is perceived to be already elevated. This paper estimates the macroeconomic and financial effects of fiscal risk shocks using a novel identification from bond yields. We first recover country-specific fiscal risk shocks from a daily Bayesian VAR model in sovereign and safe corporate bond yields, identified via contemporaneous sign restrictions that capture portfolio rebalancing away from government debt toward private safe assets. We then estimate the effects of these shocks using a local-projections framework applied to a monthly panel of twelve economies. Fiscal risk shocks generate stagflationary dynamics. Inflation and inflation expectations rise on impact, while industrial production increases only temporarily before declining persistently. Sovereign yield curves steepen, exchange rates depreciate and equity prices fall.
papers.reason: Using a novel bond-yield identification, the paper demonstrates that fiscal risk shocks trigger stagflationary dynamics, currency depreciation, and equity declines across a panel of economies.

papers.title: Public debt and monetary policy transmission: evidence from advanced and emerging Europe
papers.abstract: Using high-frequency euro area monetary policy shocks and panel local projections for the period 2001-2020, this paper examines how macroeconomic variables respond based on the level and the maturity structure of public debt.
papers.reason: Evaluates how public debt levels and maturity structures affect monetary policy transmission using euro area policy shocks, offering direct inputs for rates and sovereign debt strategies.

papers.title: Nowcasting Economic Activity in Afghanistan
papers.abstract: Sound economic policy formulation requires high frequency economic activity data. This is particularly challenging in low-income, fragile, and conflict-affected states, such as Afghanistan, where quarterly GDP data is unavailable and annual GDP figures are published with considerable delays. This paper utilizes an innovative approach for estimating quarterly economic activity under these constraints, facilitating timely economic assessments in Afghanistan. Quarterly GDP data are interpolated from annual figures, utilizing money supply as a proxy indicator of economic activities due to Afghanistan’s predominately cash-based economy. By leveraging machine learning, traditional (macroeconomic), non-traditional (satellite) data, the approach provides real-time insights of the underlying direction of the Afghan economy at relatively high frequency and with partial information.
papers.reason: Develops a nowcasting framework for GDP in Afghanistan using money supply and machine learning, offering niche utility for fragile economies.

papers.title: Alternative Trade Corridors of the GCC
papers.abstract: We provide the first quantitative general-equilibrium assessment of the trade and welfare effects of the India–Middle East–Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC), a proposed rail-to-sea trade route through the Arabian Peninsula. We translate changes in transit times and transportation cost into bilateral trade costs and use them to inform a structural gravity counterfactual for over 200 countries and territories. We estimate that the declines in trade costs from IMEC would be modest, averaging 3.6 percent among affected pairs. Our results indicate that IMEC would benefit the GCC countries and Jordan most, with these countries gaining from the enhanced overland connectivity and more direct access to trade partners in Europe, North America, and North Africa. Upper- and lower-bound scenarios highlight the nonlinear role of relative rail and sea freight rates and the value of time in determining the corridor’s effectiveness, while additional sensitivity exercises show that transit delays can substantially reduce route adoption and the resulting gains.
papers.reason: Evaluates the trade and welfare effects of the IMEC trade route across 200 countries, identifying regional winners in the GCC and Jordan.

papers.title: Global Pension Reform Database 1952 – 2025
papers.abstract: This paper introduces the Global Pension Reform Database (GPRD), the first dataset to provide systematic coverage of pension reforms across 142 advanced, emerging, and developing economies from 1952 to 2025. Leveraging artificial intelligence (AI) through a ring-fenced, locally hosted large language model (LLM), we extract and classify more than 4,000 pension reform episodes from the Economist Intelligence Unit and the U.S. Social Security Administration by type, timing, status, and generosity, enabling consistent cross-country and historical analysis. Stylized facts show that pension reform has shifted from an advanced-economy phenomenon to a global and recurring policy tool, often clustered around fiscal and macroeconomic crises. An empirical application demonstrates its analytical potential: in non-advanced economies, implemented pension reforms are associated with statistically significant and persistent declines in the public debt-to-GDP ratio, suggesting that such reforms can contribute to sustained fiscal consolidation.
papers.reason: Introduces a global pension reform dataset spanning 142 economies and demonstrates that reforms help reduce public debt ratios in non-advanced economies.

papers.title: Are European Firms Financially Constrained?
papers.abstract: We examine if European firms face binding financial constraints that explain Europe’s persistent scale-up gap. Using corporate tax changes as exogenous shocks and a "debt test", we analyze 7 million predominantly private firms across 20 euro area countries (2000–2022). A higher corporate tax rate increases the value of interest deductibility and, absent frictions, induces firms to increase leverage. We find that firms generally increase leverage after tax hikes, indicating constraints are not broadly binding. However, young firms and those in innovation-intensive industries show weaker responses. Among innovative firms, constraints vary: young firms appear unconstrained, while small, mature ones face binding constraints. Our findings suggest that financing frictions in Europe are concentrated among specific firm types at particular development stages, indicating that they are important at the critical scale-up stage.
papers.reason: Analyzes 7 million European firms using tax changes to show that financing frictions are concentrated among small, mature innovative firms.

papers.title: A Global DSGE Model for Oil-Dependent Economies
papers.abstract: This paper develops a global DSGE model linking oil-dependent economies to the systemic economies, and applies it to the GCC countries. The model features a range of nominal and real rigidities, extensive macrofinancial linkages, and diverse spillover transmission channels. Its modular structure also encompasses common features of oil-dependent economies, including a state-owned oil company, a capital intensive oil extraction technology, a sovereign wealth fund, an oil consumption subsidy, and membership of an international oil cartel. The calibrated model is used to simulate global risk and domestic reform scenarios the GCC economies, revealing how their distinct structural characteristics shape their responses to shocks.
papers.reason: Constructs a global DSGE model tailored to oil-dependent economies and GCC structures to simulate global shocks and structural reforms.

papers.title: On the Role and Effectiveness of Fiscal Rules and Independent Fiscal Councils
papers.abstract: Fiscal rules and fiscal councils are often adopted independently: many countries operate under fiscal rules without a fiscal council, while fiscal councils are frequently established only after a fiscal rule is already in place, suggesting that the two institutions may contribute differently to fiscal discipline. This paper starts with a simple theoretical framework to explain these stylized facts, accounting for the fact that governments, or even society at large, may not always be in favour of a fiscal council. The model also predicts that a sufficient strengthening of a budget balance rule, an independent fiscal council, and an increased interaction between rule strength and council strength all help reduce the expected deficit. The ensuing empirical analysis, using the updated 2025 IMF datasets on fiscal rules and fiscal councils, tests these predictions for a large country sample, including 32 advanced economies and 58 emerging market and developing economies spanning from 2000 to 2024. We find indicative evidence that, depending on the sample and the institutional design, both stronger rules and councils are associated with lower primary deficits, reduced projection biases and improved forecast accuracy. We also find some role for the interaction between the strengths of rules and councils, although the pattern varies.
papers.reason: This paper evaluates the impact of fiscal rules and independent councils on primary deficits across 90 countries, offering useful inputs for sovereign risk and fiscal sustainability assessments.

papers.title: Options for Tax System Reform in Asia and the Pacific
papers.abstract: Asian and Pacific economies face mounting fiscal pressures from high and rising debt and interest rates and significant spending needs in light of successive shocks. In the coming years, these fiscal strains will likely be exacerbated by the fiscal implications of structural trends in demography, technology, geoeconomic fragmentation, and climate transitions. To address these mounting fiscal challenges, domestic revenue mobilization will be imperative. Based on a comparative analysis with global peers, this paper provides an integrated assessment of the opportunities for enhanced revenue mobilization across the region, drawing on newly compiled data and indicators for cross-country revenue, tax design and tax administration. It documents comparatively low tax-to-GDP ratios and sizable tax potential, alongside marked differences in policy design and administrative capacity across income groups. The paper identifies five areas for reform for Asian and Pacific countries: strengthening value-added taxation; rationalizing corporate income tax incentives; expanding recurrent property taxation; accelerating digitalization in tax administration; and building public trust in tax administration. The appropriate sequencing differs across countries, but durable domestic revenue mobilization requires policy and administration to be treated as an integrated system, embedded in medium-term revenue strategies, and adapted to structural transitions and institutional capacity.
papers.reason: The study examines revenue mobilization and tax system reforms across Asian and Pacific economies, providing clear insights for regional fiscal sustainability and sovereign credit risk.

papers.title: The Macroeconomic Impact of AI Access Disruptions
papers.abstract: This paper estimates the macroeconomic impact from shutting off a country’s access to frontier AI services, once that country has grown to rely on them as an input to its economy. Applied through the production network framework of Baqaee and Farhi (2019) and calibrated to a representative small open economy, the headline GDP loss from “AI sanctions” is 0.20 percent. The range of possible outcomes can vary significantly, however, depending on the future convergence path of competitor models and on the substitutability of AI across sectors. In the most severe scenario, the economic impact reaches 0.41 percent of GDP.
papers.reason: Using a production network model calibrated to a small open economy, the paper estimates modest GDP losses from cutting off frontier AI access.

papers.title: Deconstructing the Stablecoin Sandwich
papers.abstract: Stablecoins are presented as a low-cost alternative to traditional cross-border payment channels, but evidence to support this claim remains limited. We develop a cost accounting framework that traces the full “stablecoin sandwich'”: fiat in, stablecoin transfer, fiat out. We manually collect data on costs from publicly available information across 270 directed corridors covering 18 countries, 29 exchanges, and over 4,000 complete routes. Assuming users select the cheapest options for fiat on- and off- ramps, we estimate that the average cost of a $200 transfer is around 2 percent across all corridors, below the G20 target of 3 percent and cheaper than traditional remittances on average. However, in roughly one-third of corridors where granular information on costs through traditional routes is available, the cheapest traditional provider offers a lower cost than the cheapest stablecoin route. Trading fees and fiat rail (on- and off-ramp) fees account for the majority of total costs, while the stablecoin premium—the deviation of local exchange prices of stablecoins from benchmark exchange rates—is the primary driver of cross-corridor variation, pushing costs below zero in some corridors and above 8 percent in others.
papers.reason: By collecting cross-corridor cost data for stablecoin transfers, this paper provides empirical evidence on alternative payment channels relevant for FX and cross-border capital flows.

papers.title: Rethinking Zombie Firms
papers.abstract: The literature characterizes zombie firms as economically unviable companies that continue to operate. This paper proposes that the majority of zombie firms can be viable, with positive continuation value, and arise endogenously from productivity shocks. Drawing on firm-level data covering the universe of Canadian firms and seven European countries, we document five stylized facts: zombie firms are widespread, unprofitable, unproductive, micro-sized, and transitory. We rationalize these findings by building a general equilibrium model of heterogeneous firms that abstracts from the conventional distortions thought to explain zombie firms. We show that standard productivity shocks are sufficient to explain the empirical patterns, and that the volatility of these shocks can be a key determinant of viable zombie firms, generating shares up to 35%. Since this volatility can also raise aggregate productivity and household utility, the presence of zombie firms is not a sufficient condition for lower welfare. Using a model-based definition to distinguish viability, we find limited evidence—around 0.25%—of unviable zombie firms in the data. Our results challenge the prevailing view that persistently weak firms are unviable and suggest that existing zombie firm measures likely capture viable firms.
papers.reason: This firm-level study challenges conventional views on corporate zombies by showing most are viable entities driven by productivity shocks, with indirect implications for corporate credit.

papers.title: Macroeconomic Effects of Forced Displacement in Sub-Saharan Africa
papers.abstract: This paper estimates the macroeconomic effects of forced displacement on host economies in SubSaharan Africa, drawing on cross-country panel data and country case studies of Burkina Faso, South Sudan, and Uganda to provide granular evidence on the consequences of spatial concentrations of forcibly displaced persons within countries. Estimates from a difference-in-differences local projections (LP-DiD) framework do not suggest that large refugee inflows significantly affect host-country GDP, inflation, or the current account balance over a five-year horizon. The effects on the primary fiscal balance also appear to be muted, yet this masks offsetting fiscal dynamics: government expenditures rise and fiscal revenues increase (mainly through taxes). These results are robust to restricting the control group to Sub-Saharan African economies. Under a broader treatment definition that captures the total displaced population (refugees and internally displaced persons), the GDP response turns significantly negative and intensifies with displacement severity, though this estimate is best interpreted as an upper bound because it cannot be fully separated from the effects of conflict itself that generates displacement. The cross-country findings are consistent with the case studies, which indicate generally muted effects on aggregate food inflation and wages. Beneath this muted aggregate response, however, a consistent pattern emerges across cases: prices of imported and processed staples rise, while those of locally produced cereals stay flat or fall. The case studies also yield mixed evidence regarding the impacts of displacement inflows on consumption and labor force participation, with such inflows reducing host employment in Burkina Faso but raising it in Uganda.
papers.reason: The paper estimates the macroeconomic and fiscal effects of forced displacement in Sub-Saharan Africa, finding generally muted aggregate impacts on GDP and inflation.

papers.title: Global Spillovers from U.S. Bond Supply Shocks
papers.abstract: I study spillovers from U.S. bond supply shocks, identified from yield moves around U.S. Treasury auction announcements. Using the shocks as instruments in daily and monthly local projections for AEs and EMs, I find substantial pass-through to global long-term rates. A debt expansion shock that raises the U.S. 10-year yield by 10 bps lifts foreign 10-year yields by roughly 7 bps within a few business days. Monthly aggregation shows contractionary real effects: U.S. industrial production falls up to 0.4 percent after eight months and foreign industrial production by a comparable amount, around 0.4 percent, with a more persistent profile. The foreign contraction reflects financial tightening, exchange-rate depreciation, and weaker U.S. demand. Spillovers are heterogeneous: moving from the 25th to 75th percentile of foreign investor participation deepens the IP decline by 0.5 pp. Results are robust to a demand-side shock and consistent with the relevant benchmarks, highlighting U.S. bond supply as a key driver of global financial conditions and real activity, amplified by foreign investor participation and weak domestic fundamentals.
papers.reason: This paper directly informs global rates, FX, and sovereign debt markets by demonstrating that U.S. bond supply shocks spill over significantly to foreign long-term yields and industrial activity.

papers.title: The EU’s Energy Transition and Fuel Price Shocks
papers.abstract: This paper analyzes how achieving Europe’s medium-term greenhouse gas mitigation targets enhances energy security, defined as the cushioning of the adverse macroeconomic impact of oil and gas price shocks. It uses the IMF’s Global Macroeconomic Model of the Energy Transition, which combines a rich set of New-Keynesian features with a detailed representation of fossil fuel use, including granular modelling of the transport and heating sectors. Future oil and gas price shocks are simulated in a scenario where Europe’s mitigation policy agenda has been fully implemented (and mitigation targets are met), and in a hypothetical scenario where mitigation policy has remained constant at the current level of ambition. A comparison shows that the policy agenda substantially dampens future shock transmission. The inflationary impact of both shocks is close to 40 percent larger under constant policies than under the mitigation agenda, and for oil shocks, the output decline is about twice as large. These energy security co-benefits materialize gradually as the economy adjusts to the mitigation agenda, and are shown to depend on ETS2, the new emissions trading system covering transportation and buildings. An additional exercise proxies for merit-order electricity pricing. In these simulations, the mitigation agenda further reduces pass-through from gas price shocks to electricity prices, thereby enhancing the macroeconomic stabilizing effects.
papers.reason: Using a structural macro model for Europe, the paper shows how climate mitigation policies dampen the inflationary and output impacts of future oil and gas price shocks.

papers.title: Information Networks and Inflation Expectations
papers.abstract: How are inflation expectations affected by foreign supply shocks? We show that, beyond bilateral exposure, a second network matters: the one linking forecasters to the countries they cover. Using forecasterlevel expectations around conflict episodes—precisely dated supply shocks that raise inflation through trade and energy linkages—we find that expectations are revised upward gradually in the days following a conflict. Within the same country and day, forecasters who cover the conflict country revise by 0.2 to 0.3 percentage points less than those who do not, and the differential roughly triples where bilateral exposure is highest. We rationalize this in a model where a public narrative overstates spillovers in proportion to bilateral exposure, and only forecasters covering the conflict country can discount it. The consensus therefore inherits a bias largest where exposure is high and coverage thin, and a central bank reading it at face value tightens more than fundamentals warrant.
papers.reason: The paper provides empirical evidence on how information networks and public narratives shape forecaster expectations during supply shocks, directly relevant for monetary policy and inflation pricing.

papers.title: Understanding Over-Optimism in Tax Revenue-to-GDP Forecasts under IMF-supported Programs
papers.abstract: Revenue mobilization is a key objective in many IMF-supported programs, yet tax revenue-to-GDP forecasts often fall short of outcomes. This paper analyzes the underlying drivers of these forecast misses by leveraging two novel global datasets on tax policy yields and tax administration capacity. It finds that tax revenue-to-GDP forecast errors are primarily driven by over-optimism in forecasted yields of tax policy measures and tax buoyancy assumptions, as well as macroeconomic forecast errors, particularly for growth and trade openness. Stronger tax administration capacity and well-implemented and high-quality revenue related structural reforms are associated with lower forecast errors.
