papers.title: Cash Transfers in Developing Countries: Local Multipliers, Aggregate Effects, and External Adjustment
papers.abstract: This paper studies the local and aggregate effects of cash transfers in developing countries, and how both change as the cash transfer program scales up. We build a two-region New Keynesian small open economy model and calibrate it to rich pre-treatment microdata from an ongoing cash transfer experiment in Malawi. The model implies a local multiplier on temporary transfers of about one, which depends on price stickiness, the share of liquidity-constrained households, and home bias in consumption. Spillovers to the rest of the country are negative under Malawi’s restricted international capital mobility and parallel exchange rate regimes, as cash transfers appreciate the real exchange rate and reduce exports. Consequently, the aggregate multiplier is less than the local multiplier. As the program scales up, the local multiplier converges toward the aggregate multiplier, so a scaled-up program may have smaller multipliers than micro-level estimates suggest. However, with unrestricted capital mobility, spillovers can be positive, especially under a fixed exchange rate. These results highlight the importance of the macroeconomic policy environment for aggregate multipliers and the effects of scaled-up transfer programs.
papers.reason: Examines cash transfer multipliers and exchange rate spillovers in developing economies using Malawi data, offering clear insights for emerging market macro policy.

papers.title: In Hot Water? The Macroeconomic Impacts of El Niño
papers.abstract: Despite their potentially major impacts, little is known about how El Niño impact the U.S. economy. El Niños are distinct from other commonly studied weather shocks because they are a global phenomenon, unfold over a period of months, can be forecast months in advance, are relatively infrequent, and have very different effects on weather outcomes depending on the time of year and region. These features make traditional analytical methods ill-suited to studying the economic impacts of El Niño events. In this paper I use a new approach to estimating the impulse response functions of El Niños. I find that El Niños pose material upside risk for PCE prices and employment. The longer-run price effects are driven by core services and food prices and depend on whether La Niñas follow El Niños, a very common occurrence. After modest offsetting initial effects, employment increases are widespread in terms of both sectors and states in the year following the El Niño. These results indicate El Niños can have material impacts on the US economy even though it is neither tropical nor agriculturally focused.
papers.reason: Provides empirical estimates of El Niño impacts on US inflation and employment, offering useful cyclical inputs for rates and inflation forecasters.

papers.title: Bank Regulation Affects Monetary Policy Transmission
papers.abstract: How does monetary policy impact banks’ lending behavior when interest rate changes revalue their securities? Detailed supervisory data show that banks with larger losses on securities during the 2022–23 monetary policy tightening cycle extended less credit to firms. This spillover effect was especially strong for securities that were marked to market and not hedged, and for banks required to include unrealized losses in regulatory capital. These conditions lead to larger reductions in corporate debt and investment, increasing monetary policy’s impact on the economy.
papers.reason: Directly evaluates how bank regulation and unrealized securities losses affected credit extension during the recent US tightening cycle, informing banking and monetary policy views.

papers.title: Pricing Inflation Swaps in the Japanese Bond Market
papers.abstract: Japanese government bond markets present a puzzling pattern. Unlike U.S. markets, where bond liquidity and other premiums have been shown to drive a wedge between prices of nominal U.S. Treasury securities and those of matching portfolios comprised of inflation-indexed bonds and derivative contracts, analysis shows no such wedge for similar asset combinations in Japanese markets.
papers.reason: The analysis of pricing dynamics and absence of liquidity wedges in Japanese inflation-linked assets is directly relevant for rates and inflation-swaps trading desks.

papers.title: What Do Financial Officers Predict for the Labor Market?
papers.abstract: Business leader surveys can be an important and reliable source for insights into future labor market conditions, particularly for expected wage growth. Survey responses from financial executives regarding their expectations for wages at their firms have closely tracked subsequent actual U.S. nominal wage growth since 2002, outperforming household survey projections in their accuracy. Estimates for this year point to continued nominal wage growth in 2026. Respondents also expect employment growth to moderate, though their projections reflect uncertainty regarding potential gains in workers’ purchasing power.
papers.reason: Analyzes financial executive surveys to track expected US wage and employment growth, providing timely indicators for inflation and monetary policy.

papers.title: Effects of Oil Supply Disruptions on Oil Exporters, Importers
papers.abstract: Economies may face different challenges during oil supply disruptions depending on whether they primarily import or export oil. Comparing the effects of past disruptions in Canada, a large net oil exporter, and the euro area, a large oil importer, suggests that both experienced rising inflation and declining economic activity. This reflects that the energy sector accounts for a small share of GDP, while oil prices affect global demand and nonenergy sectors. Thus, benefits to the energy sector from higher oil prices were outweighed by the costs to the broader economy.
papers.reason: Compares the macroeconomic impact of oil supply disruptions on exporters and importers, informing FX and inflation expectations.

papers.title: Stablecoin Issuers’ Growing Appetite for Treasury Securities
papers.abstract: Over the past 20 years, the share of U.S. debt held by foreigners has fallen substantially. Demand for U.S. debt has partly shifted towards private investors, including from novel sources, particularly stablecoin issuers. The increase in stablecoins’ holdings of Treasury securities has helped partly offset the demand decline from some foreign governments. While their share of holdings is relatively small, if the trend continues, stablecoin issuers’ demand for short-term Treasury securities could nearly double to a more noteworthy $400 billion by the end of 2030.
papers.reason: Quantifies stablecoin issuers' growing demand for short-term U.S. Treasuries, offering direct insight into structural shifts in sovereign debt absorption.

papers.title: Risk Appetite and Monetary Transmission
papers.abstract: We construct a new high-frequency measure of risk appetite shifts around Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meetings, the common component of changes in risk-sensitive indicators. Fed policy actions and communication have substantial effects on risk appetite. Interest-rate surprises explain only about one-fifth of the variation in risk appetite, so most policy-induced changes in risk asset prices are orthogonal to the expected rate path. We therefore use both surprises as external instruments in a proxy SVAR with two separately identified shocks. Risk appetite shocks have large and persistent contractionary effects, lowering output and prices while raising unemployment. By contrast, the effects of risk-free rate shocks tend to be small and imprecisely estimated, and some have puzzling signs. Monetary transmission appears to operate primarily through risk appetite and risk asset prices. Estimates relying on interest-rate surprises alone miss most of these effects, for two reasons: the link from interest rates to risk appetite is state-dependent, and Fed communication moves it independently of the expected rate path.
papers.reason: Directly informs rates and FX strategists by demonstrating that US monetary transmission operates primarily through risk appetite and asset prices rather than standard rate paths.

papers.title: How AI Adoption Might Affect Bank Lending
papers.abstract: Commercial banks have led the adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) in recent years. Evidence suggests that banks using AI more intensively tend to have higher returns on assets and higher shares of problem loans. Increased AI usage is also associated with declines in the shares of small business lending. This pattern suggests that AI helps banks in processing hard data, such as credit scores and financial statements, and issuing fewer small business loans that rely more on soft information, such as personal and business relationships.
papers.reason: The study links bank AI adoption to changes in loan portfolios and credit availability for small businesses, informing banking sector dynamics.

papers.title: Consumer Vibe Check: Gas Prices and Inflation Expectations
papers.abstract: According to household surveys, inflation expectations tend to move together with expectations for gasoline price changes. The relationship is not symmetrical, though: Inflation expectations rise when households revise up their outlook for gas price growth but change little when they revise it down. This pattern is strongest among lower-income and less-educated households. Analysis also suggests that increases in expected gas price growth are associated with greater perceived inflation uncertainty. However, quantitatively, the evidence suggests a moderate relationship between changes in expected gasoline prices and households’ inflation expectations.
papers.reason: The study links gasoline price perceptions to household inflation expectations, providing useful color on consumer pricing psychology and survey measures.

papers.title: Can Fiscal, AI, or Monetary News Explain the Rise in r∗?
papers.abstract: Following decades of secular decline, many estimates of r∗—the natural or steady-state short-term real interest rate—have risen roughly 1 percentage point since 2020 in the United States. The most prominent explanations attribute this reversal to heightened expectations of rising government debt and faster productivity growth from artificial intelligence (AI). However, a high-frequency event study finds that news about fiscal and AI developments does not explain this increase. Furthermore, contrary to earlier evidence that persistent shifts in longer-term yields occurred around monetary policy meetings, we find that monetary policy news does not account for the recent rise in r∗.
papers.reason: Using high-frequency event studies, it evaluates popular market narratives regarding the post-2020 rise in US r*, directly challenging assumptions around fiscal, AI, and monetary drivers.

papers.title: Quality, Inequality and Understanding Housing Markets
papers.abstract: Most housing research relies on a single-margin model where a single housing price relates to a single housing quantity. We generalize this approach by introducing income inequality and housing quality. Two important challenges to studying housing supply (and demand) emerge: First, there is no singular housing supply function, instead there is a continuum of unit-supply functions indexed by quality. This implies that supply elasticity estimates are local average treatment effects (LATEs), not structural elasticities. Second, spillovers common in spatial settings may preclude even the LATE interpretation of estimates, which are instead local general equilibrium objects. Critically, these issues cannot be bypassed by using the land share of value to measure supply constraints as it is not even a diagnostic for supply constraints in the standard model. We suggest that understanding heterogeneity in incomes and housing services quality is likely critical to understanding housing markets more generally.
papers.reason: It introduces a theoretical critique of standard housing supply and elasticity estimates incorporating income inequality, providing indirect methodological guidance for real estate and mortgage market analysis.

papers.title: What’s Behind the Declining Trend Unemployment Rate?
papers.abstract: The U.S. unemployment rate has trended down for decades. Estimates after removing business cycle fluctuations show that the trend rate fell from 7.8% in 1976 to 4.8% in 2024. This decline reflects in part a more-educated and older workforce—that is, a shift in composition towards demographic groups with traditionally lower unemployment rates. It also reflects newer cohorts entering the labor force with lower unemployment rates. Projections suggest that future demographic changes will gradually lower trend unemployment about 0.4 percentage point further over the next 20 years.
papers.reason: Examines structural declines in the US trend unemployment rate driven by demographics, offering useful context for long-term macroeconomic projections.

papers.title: Assessing a Medium-Run Natural Rate of Interest
papers.abstract: The natural rate of interest is the inflation-adjusted interest rate consistent with the economy operating at full capacity. Although this rate helps gauge the economy’s health, empirical estimates of it are imprecise and volatile. A medium-run measure that focuses on responsiveness to persistent economic factors while removing short-term volatility may provide more reliable guidance. Analysis suggests that monetary policy using this measure could stabilize inflation and achieve maximum employment more effectively than standard benchmarks. Current medium-run estimates suggest that monetary policy is accommodative, although uncertainty around this estimate remains high.
papers.reason: Directly informs monetary policy assessment and interest rate expectations by analyzing a medium-run measure of the neutral rate.

papers.title: Financial Markets, Oil Prices, and Supply-Side Risks
papers.abstract: The relation between stocks and bonds indicates whether supply or demand shocks dominate the risks to economic activity. After two decades of concerns primarily about changes in demand, the stock-bond correlation recently flipped, suggesting that the perceived source of risk to the economy has shifted towards supply shocks. Other financial correlations, such as the stock-oil correlation, also changed accordingly and thus agree with this interpretation. In line with this evidence, financial market pricing now indicates that elevated oil prices and potential inflation are prominent sources of risk.
papers.reason: The paper links changes in stock-bond and stock-oil correlations directly to shifting macroeconomic risk perceptions from demand to supply shocks, informing multi-asset strategy.

papers.title: Reaching for Duration
papers.abstract: Using historical data on U.S. commercial bank balance sheets, we show that banks’ maturity mismatch has more than tripled since the mid-1980s, moving in close lockstep with declining interest rates and term premia. We rationalize these trends in a model of bank portfolio choice in which banks must cover operating costs out of current earnings. When term premia or short-term rates decline, banks extend the duration of their assets to remain profitable. This “reaching for duration” effect is convex in the degree of term premium compression. The resulting maturity mismatch renders banks increasingly vulnerable to self-fulfilling runs by uninsured depositors. Consistent with the model, less profitable banks subsequently raise their asset maturities, particularly in periods of low term premia and large Federal Reserve asset holdings. Quantitative easing, designed to remove duration risk from the private sector, may thus paradoxically concentrate it on bank balance sheets and undermine financial stability.
papers.reason: The study demonstrates how declining term premia drive commercial banks to extend asset duration, increasing vulnerability to runs and carrying direct implications for banking stability and monetary transmission.

papers.title: Will AI Intensify or Weaken Market Competition?
papers.abstract: We study how AI affects market competition based on a general equilibrium framework with heterogeneous firms facing idiosyncratic productivity and variable markups. Firms choose the AI technology subject to fixed costs, where AI production requires data and energy inputs. Our model predicts a non-monotonic relation of AI diffusion with industry concentration. As AI usage rises from an initially low level, large incumbent users gain market share. When AI usage is sufficiently diffused, entry of new and smaller adopters erodes the market share of incumbents, reducing industry concentration. The non-monotonic relations are robust when firms can complement AI with their own data. Our calibrated model predicts that industry concentration is likely to fall if AI adoption increases relative to the current level. In comparison, the relation of AI with the average markup depends on whether increased AI usage is driven by demand or supply factors. Our model also predicts that a modest subsidy of about 3 percent for AI adopter revenues maximizes social welfare, reflecting a tradeoff between aggregate productivity and the average markup associated with AI usage.
papers.reason: The paper uses a theoretical general equilibrium framework to model AI adoption and industry concentration, offering conceptual insights for structural equity analysis rather than immediate trading signals.

papers.title: Job-Finding Anomalies of the Current Expansion
papers.abstract: Job-finding rates have declined over the past three years for people who are unemployed or are out of the labor force. Analysis shows that the decline in job finding for unemployed people has been pronounced for prime-age and college-educated individuals, while the decline in job finding for people who are out of the labor force has been driven by younger and less-educated individuals. These demographic patterns differ from job-finding rates during typical economic expansions and imply both a cooling and a restructuring within the labor market.
papers.reason: The analysis of recent job-finding anomalies across demographics provides clear insight into US labor market cooling and restructuring, directly informing monetary policy and macro views.

papers.title: AI Adoption Among Small Businesses: Qualitative Insights from the Small Business Credit Survey
papers.abstract: Nearly 40% of small business respondents to the 2024 Small Business Credit Survey (SBCS) reported either using or planning to use artificial intelligence (AI), revealing a rapidly evolving landscape of adoption among the nation’s smaller firms. Sentiments around AI adoption ranged from enthusiasm to opposition. Reported applications of AI among small business respondents were just as varied, spanning both core operations and support functions. Common applications included: -productivity tasks -marketing, social media, and search engine optimization -developing written communications -visuals generation and graphic design -customer service -analytics and forecasting -programming machines and sensors -developing custom AI tools for specific business needs The sophistication of these applications varied considerably, from basic task assistance to complex, integrated systems. Many firms expressed interest in AI adoption but reported facing barriers, including policy and regulatory limitations, financial costs associated with appropriate tools, time and capacity constraints related to staff training and system upgrades, and knowledge gaps regarding implementation strategies. Other firms deliberately opted not to adopt AI, citing concerns about accuracy and intellectual property rights, the centrality of human interaction to their business model, or an absence of perceived applicability to their operations. These findings from the 2024 SBCS’s initial qualitative inquiry into AI adoption establish a baseline understanding of how small businesses are experiencing this technological transformation and complement forthcoming analysis of the 2025 SBCS, which included a comprehensive supplemental survey module on AI adoption.
papers.reason: Provides qualitative survey evidence on AI adoption among US small businesses with only indirect implications for productivity and broader macroeconomic trends.

papers.title: Prices and Monetary Policy: The Role of Financial Constraints
papers.abstract: Firm heterogeneity in financial constraints is a quantitatively important driver of how monetary policy transmits to inflation. Using detailed microdata on Swedish public and private firms, and high-frequency monetary policy surprises around Riksbank announcements, we document that smaller, financially constrained firms adjust prices significantly less than larger firms in response to changes in monetary policy. This heterogeneous price response materially dampens the aggregate PPI inflation response to monetary policy. Models of customer markets and financial frictions can explain our findings: because the external finance premium rises after a monetary contraction, constrained firms cut prices less to preserve cash flows, sacrificing future market share. Additional evidence on heterogeneous sales, debt, marginal cost, and markup responses further supports this channel. We consider several alternative explanations, including differences in price adjustments, working capital, market share, and export share, but these cannot rationalize our main heterogeneity result.
papers.reason: Demonstrates using Swedish firm-level data that financial constraints drive heterogeneous price adjustments, altering the aggregate inflation response to monetary policy shocks.

papers.title: Recency Effects in Perceived Uncertainty
papers.abstract: Firms frequently revise not only their expectations, but also how uncertain they feel about those expectations. Using the U.S. Survey of Business Uncertainty, we study perceived uncertainty about firms’ own sales and employment growth. Reported uncertainty rises after larger revisions to firms’ point forecasts, with the strongest response to the most recent revision. This recency pattern remains visible outside elevated sectoral-volatility episodes. We develop a model in which agents learn about a constant-volatility process but recall older observations noisily. Noisy recall gives recent surprises disproportionate influence, even when objective volatility is constant.
papers.reason: Studies recency bias in US firms' perceived sales and employment uncertainty using survey data, offering limited direct utility for near-term macro trading strategies.

papers.title: Firms’ Inflation Expectations During the Pandemic-Era Surge
papers.abstract: Inflation expectations among businesses can affect how they set current prices. Firms’ expectations diverged from those of professional forecasters during the pandemic-era inflation surge and moved closer to household expectations. Analyzing firms’ survey data from 2018 to 2025 reveals three main patterns behind this shift: Businesses became more sensitive to current inflation perceptions, their longer-term expectations temporarily drifted up, and their perceptions of the Federal Reserve’s inflation goal increased. However, when inflation eventually moderated, the survey data show that firms’ inflation expectations largely returned to their characteristics from before the pandemic.
papers.reason: Analyzes US business survey data to show how firm inflation expectations shifted during the pandemic surge and subsequently normalized, informing monetary policy and price-setting dynamics.

papers.title: Using Inflation Shock Patterns to Help Forecast Inflation
papers.abstract: A new indicator—the Inflation Shock Momentum Index—can help identify emerging inflationary or disinflationary pressures in real time. The index tracks the shares of consumer spending categories that are experiencing consecutive positive or negative monthly inflation shocks, allowing detection of shifts in the underlying inflation environment. The index improves inflation forecasts at one-year to three-year horizons and responds to macroeconomic shocks in line with accepted theory. Recent index readings have fluctuated above and below zero, indicating that inflation may remain near current levels in the near to medium term.
papers.reason: The paper introduces a real-time indicator that improves inflation forecasts at medium-term horizons, directly informing interest rate and fixed income strategies.

papers.title: The Tipping Point: Interest Rates and Financial Stability
papers.abstract: Abstract This paper studies the impact of interest rates on bank stability in a standard bank‐run model. Banks invest in long‐term assets, whose value decreases with interest rates, and set deposit rates to optimally insure depositors' liquidity risk. Liquidity‐risk insurance implies banks earn interest margins, which increase with interest rates. Hence, interest rates have two countervailing effects: they reduce the value of banks' long‐term assets while widening their margins. First, the paper characterizes the parametric condition under which an effect dominates. The condition implies interest‐rate risk is captured by banks' maturity mismatch adjusted for deposits' effective duration. Second, the paper solves for the interest‐rate level that tips banks into instability. Quantification points to the possibility of a negative effective maturity mismatch, making the tipping point a lower bound on interest rates.
papers.reason: This paper models the trade-off between higher interest rates and bank asset values versus net interest margins, directly informing banking sector stability and monetary transmission.

analysis.summary: This paper examines how interest rate changes affect bank stability using a theoretical bank-run framework. Higher interest rates exert two opposing pressures on banks: they decrease the value of long-term assets while increasing net interest margins earned on deposit insurance provision. The net impact depends on a bank's maturity mismatch adjusted for the effective duration of deposits. Under certain conditions, such as a negative effective maturity mismatch, the critical threshold for bank instability acts as a lower bound on interest rates. This indicates that excessively low interest rates, rather than high rates, may present the primary risk to financial stability in specific structural settings.
key_takeaways: Interest rates affect bank stability via two opposing mechanisms: reducing long-term asset values while expanding net interest margins derived from liquidity-risk insurance.
The dominant effect is determined by a bank's maturity mismatch adjusted for the effective duration of its deposit base.
Quantitative findings highlight that a negative effective maturity mismatch can turn the financial stability tipping point into a lower bound on policy interest rates.
analysis.relevance: This research informs debates on central bank policy rate paths, bank equity valuations, and financial stability monitoring. Financial strategists and rates analysts can apply the concept of effective maturity mismatch—factoring in deposit duration—to assess bank balance sheet vulnerability across different rate regimes. It suggests that prolonged low interest rate environments may pose greater structural risks to banking solvency than rate hikes when deposit stickiness provides substantial duration cushioning.
analysis.market_focus_rationale: The paper develops a theoretical bank-run model and quantitative exercise without restricting its framework or data to a specific country or market dataset.

papers.title: Derivative margin calls: A new driver of MMF flows
papers.abstract: The COVID-19 market turmoil triggered significant outflows from euro area money market funds (MMFs), reaching nearly 8% of assets under management. By analysing granular data on derivative contracts and MMF activity, we identify a novel shock transmission mechanism: as financial intermediaries use MMFs as cash management vehicles, derivative margin calls can generate MMF flows. Our findings suggest that margin calls faced by euro area non-bank financial intermediaries drove around 45% of the aggregate outflows from EUR-denominated euro area MMFs between February and April 2020, revealing a critical channel through which market shocks propagate.
papers.reason: The paper identifies derivative margin calls as a primary driver of euro area MMF outflows, offering direct insights for liquidity and financial stability.

analysis.summary: During the COVID-19 market turmoil in early 2020, euro area money market funds (MMFs) experienced redemptions reaching nearly 8% of assets under management. Analyzing granular transaction data, this study identifies a novel shock transmission channel: non-bank financial intermediaries use MMFs as cash management vehicles. When market volatility triggers derivative margin calls, these institutions redeem MMF holdings to fulfill cash demands. The authors find that margin calls faced by euro area non-bank financial intermediaries accounted for roughly 45% of total outflows from euro-denominated euro area MMFs between February and April 2020, highlighting strong linkages between derivatives markets and fund flows.
key_takeaways: Euro area money market funds experienced outflows of nearly 8% of assets under management during the COVID-19 market shock between February and April 2020.
Derivative margin calls on euro area non-bank financial intermediaries drove approximately 45% of aggregate outflows from EUR-denominated money market funds in early 2020.
Non-bank financial intermediaries use money market funds as cash management vehicles, creating a direct transmission channel from derivative market shocks to fund redemptions.
analysis.relevance: This paper highlights systemic linkages between derivative margin requirements and short-term money market fund liquidity in the euro area. It informs central bank policy debates regarding non-bank financial intermediation, liquidity buffers, and MMF structural reform. Money market and rates strategists can use these empirical insights to better anticipate fund redemption pressures and liquidity friction during periods of sharp derivative market repricing and heightened margin calls.
analysis.market_focus_rationale: The paper relies exclusively on data from euro area non-bank financial intermediaries and EUR-denominated euro area money market funds.

papers.title: Climate Risk and Sustainable Finance: Bridging Policy, Research and Practice
papers.abstract: The implications of climate change and the transition to a low-carbon economy extend to the economy and the financial system, making them increasingly relevant issues for central banks and supervisors. Their complexity makes the exchange of knowledge and experience among experts, academics and central bankers particularly important. Such dialogue helps enrich analysis and advance our understanding and management of risks that continue to pose significant analytical and data-related challenges. With the aim of fostering this exchange, on 25 March 2026, the Banco de España organised the high-level conference “Climate Risk and Sustainable Finance: Bridging Policy, Research and Practice”, together with the Network for Greening the Financial System, the Centre for Economic Transition Expertise and the Transition Pathway Initiative Centre at the London School of Economics. Many of the contributions presented at the conference have been brought together in Issue 33 of Papeles de Energía. This Banco de España publication brings together these contributions, offering different perspectives on the key challenges posed by climate change and the transition for the economy and the financial system.
papers.reason: Discusses central bank perspectives on climate risk and sustainable finance, offering indirect background for financial stability and macro research.

papers.title: Deck the Charts: Christmas, Streaming, and the Return of One Catalog
papers.abstract: Popular music charts changed what they measure when streaming replaced sales. A purchase-based chart records acquisition, and a purchase extinguishes the demand it registers; a streaming chart records use, and every play counts anew. Demand that recurs on a fixed schedule for a fixed repertoire was therefore invisible to the sales-era instrument and fully visible to its successor. Using daily Spotify Top 200 charts for Germany (2017-2025) matched to audio features, and weekly chart data spanning 1977-2025, we show that seasonality in the acoustic character of charted music is a phenomenon of the streaming era: absent before 2015, growing steadily since, and dominated by Christmas. On December 24 streaming volume reached 4.6 times the annual daily mean in 2024, up from 2.9 in 2017, and the charts shift sharply toward high acousticness and low energy. The pattern is selective across twenty holidays: Easter, which shares Christmas's family character, produces no acoustic effect at all, while New Year's Eve moves the charts in the opposite direction. The December peak is carried by a fixed and aging catalog, but age is that catalog's property rather than its cause: on an ordinary day old recordings are less acoustic and more energetic than contemporary releases, so a shift in age composition alone would move December the wrong way. The December component of any series built from these charts therefore reflects the recirculation of a fixed historical catalog rather than contemporary listening, with direct consequences for the seasonal adjustment of music-based sentiment indicators.
papers.reason: The paper analyzes holiday seasonality in streaming music charts, which has no relevance to financial markets or macroeconomic policy.

papers.title: Replication Data for: Specification Choices and the Interpretation of Predictive Evidence
papers.abstract: Two competent researchers analysing the same data can write very different headlines: news improves prediction, or no improvement is detected. We examine how defensible choices produce these findings and what each permits the researcher to claim. Using GDELT news indicators and Eurostat government-bond yields, we compare forecasts of volatility in a euro-area yield differential. Matched linear forecasts yield favourable evidence for news levels, but not after subtracting recent averages. Adding prespecified slower market summaries reduces the twenty-session forecast-error reduction from about 13.5% to 6.9%; no comparison against the expanded reference remains significant after adjustment for multiple comparisons. Controlled simulations examine interpretation when information content is known. A reporting rule can credit uninformative news with market-driven gains. With the stronger added signal and the same expanded reference, 58.0% of datasets yield detection with levels but not with deviations. This paired disagreement shows why a negative result needs a check of what the procedure detects when information is present. We connect matched comparisons and justified alternatives to controls with and without additional information in a claim–comparison protocol. The method helps researchers distinguish a supported conditional gain, dependence on specification choices and an unresolved informational question.
papers.reason: Examines predictive evidence and specification choices using euro-area bond yields and news indicators, offering methodological insights for fixed-income forecasting models.

papers.title: Supranational Banking Supervision, Credit Supply, and Risk‐Taking: European Evidence from Multi‐Country Credit Registers
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Using a novel data set of multi‐country credit registers and an institutional change from national to supranational supervision, we show that supranational banking supervision can increase credit supply while mitigating excessive risk‐taking. Supranational supervision increases credit supply only in financially stressed countries while reducing the credit supply to the riskiest (zombie) firms. These improved lending effects stem from weaker national institutions, differential national supervisory incentives, lower national supervisory abilities, and weaker national insolvency laws. Moreover, improved access to external finance from wholesale and bond markets as well as lower risk‐weighted assets allow supranationally supervised banks to expand the supply of credit. Overall, despite some supranational supervisory arbitrage, supranational supervision decreases firm‐level credit to the riskiest firms while increasing firm‐level credit availability in stressed countries without reducing it in nonstressed countries.
papers.reason: Assesses how supranational euro area banking supervision affects credit supply and risk-taking, directly relevant for bank credit and financial stability.

papers.title: Leaning against the Global Financial Cycle
papers.abstract: We investigate the impact of institutional quality on shielding emerging economies from the global financial cycle. Our findings indicate that countries with a higher rule of law, characterized by superior contract enforcement and more robust protection of property rights, experience a less severe tightening of domestic financial and macroeconomic conditions when faced with adverse global financial shocks. We explain this outcome through a simplified model that incorporates financial frictions, showing how strong institutions and effective governance alleviate collateral constraints and mitigate the effects of global financial pressures on the domestic economy. (JEL E44, E52, F32, F65, K11, K12, P14)
papers.reason: Examines how domestic institutional quality shields emerging markets from adverse global financial cycle shocks.

papers.title: Tariffs, production networks and spillovers: the case of a US-China trade war
papers.abstract: We study the short-run macroeconomic transmission of a US–China tariff war in an open economy multi-sector New Keynesian model with input–output linkages, sectoral nominal rigidities, and heterogeneous currency invoicing. A reciprocal 10 percentage-point tariff increase generates asymmetric incidence: the tariff-imposing country bears more of the inflationary burden, while the targeted country experiences the larger output contraction. Production networks amplify this contraction by propagating the shock beyond the directly tariffed bilateral margin. Currency invoicing further shapes transmission. Under heterogeneous invoicing, dollar-priced border prices weaken the expenditure-switching role of exchange rates, deepening the contraction in China relative to producer-currency pricing and altering third-country spillovers. The EA response is small in the aggregate, but only because positive trade-diversion margins are offset by weaker demand from China and multilateral adjustments. We then exploit the model’s sectoral structure by imposing tariffs on one Chinese sector at a time. Sectoral incidence is highly concentrated, but aggregate effects cannot be inferred from the directly tariffed sector alone: domestic propagation offsets own-sector gains in the US, reinforces own-sector losses in China, and leaves the EA as a net object shaped by opposing trade margins. The results show that tariff incidence depends jointly on where the tariff lands, how the shock propagates through production networks, and how invoicing governs border-price adjustment. A framework that combines these margins delivers a materially different assessment from one built on bilateral trade shares alone.
papers.reason: Models the macroeconomic transmission, inflation incidence, and output spillovers of reciprocal tariffs using a multi-sector open economy framework.

papers.title: Labor market change, income polarization and urban housing inequality: a comparative study of Italy, Spain and the United Kingdom
papers.abstract: Purpose This paper aims to explore the interaction between labor market reforms and housing policies in Italy, Spain and the UK. Design/methodology/approach By providing a comparative legal analysis of significant policy changes at the macro level and a descriptive overview of the evolution of their main economic determinants – wages and housing prices – at the micro level, the study highlights the socioeconomic impact of these reforms and their contribution to urban disparities. Findings The analysis suggests that the implementation of labor market reforms aimed at increasing flexibility and competitiveness coincided with heightened precarity, particularly for low-wage and nonstandard workers across all countries. Research limitations/implications The analysis does not address causality. Practical implications The paper suggests that stratified labor policy and work deregulation have an impact on urban inequality and wage distribution at sub-city level. Social implications The study argues that these reforms, coupled with macro-events such as the increase in global trades and the advent of ICT, might have exacerbated the socioeconomic inequalities at both national and local levels over the last decades by disfavoring less skilled workers, particularly in large cities. Originality/value The originality of the paper lies in its integrated analysis of labor-market reforms and housing policies as jointly producing urban disparities. Rather than treating wage stagnation, employment precarity and housing unaffordability as separate phenomena, the paper connects them through a comparative framework covering Italy, Spain and the UK. Its contribution is also empirical and spatial: it combines national regulatory trajectories with city-level evidence from Milan, London and Madrid, showing how macro-level reforms translate into uneven urban outcomes. This multi-scalar approach offers a distinctive perspective on the legal, economic and territorial roots of contemporary inequality.
papers.reason: Provides a comparative legal and descriptive overview of labor reforms and housing prices in Italy, Spain, and the UK with broad structural implications.

papers.title: The macroeconomic effects of purely forward-looking uncertainty shocks: Evidence from the euro area
papers.abstract: If the underlying data-generating process operates at a higher frequency than the observed data, impact restrictions in structural vector autoregressions (SVARs) become vulnerable to temporal aggregation. Building on Berger et al. (2020), I relax the zero-impact restriction used to identify forward-looking uncertainty shocks and apply the alternative scheme to euro area data. I find that such shocks are contractionary in the euro area, although their effects emerge only gradually and with a delay, unlike the macro-neutral effects reported for the U.S. The results suggest that temporal aggregation matters for identification and that the transmission of forward-looking uncertainty differs across economies.
papers.reason: Using an improved identification scheme that addresses temporal aggregation, the paper shows that forward-looking uncertainty shocks are contractionary in the euro area, informing ECB policy assessments.

papers.title: Ordinal Mixed-Effects Random Forests
papers.abstract: Abstract We introduce ordinal mixed-effect random forests (OMERF), a novel statistical method that extends random forests to handle hierarchical data with ordinal responses. OMERF retains the flexibility of tree-based ensemble methods for modeling complex relationships among categorical and continuous variables, while explicitly accounting for hierarchical dependence structures, enabling statistical inference across all data levels. A simulation study is conducted to validate the performance of the proposed method and to compare it to those of other state-of-the-art models. The application of OMERF is exemplified in two case studies. The former focuses on predicting students’ performance using data from the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) 2022, while the latter analyzes individual life satisfaction across European countries using data from the European Social Survey (ESS).
papers.reason: The paper introduces a statistical method for hierarchical ordinal data applied to student performance and life satisfaction, with no direct application to financial markets.

papers.title: Macroprudential capital buffers and firm financing conditions: Evidence from European firms
papers.abstract: This study examines the effectiveness of macroprudential capital buffers and their impact on firms’ financing conditions. Using 2015–2021 firm-level data from the ECB/EC Survey on the Access to Finance of Enterprises (SAFE), financial statements, and macroprudential data from the European Systemic Risk Board (ESRB), we find that tighter capital requirements during the pre-pandemic period are associated with higher interest costs, though loan availability is not significantly affected. During the COVID-19 crisis, the release of the countercyclical capital buffer (CCyB) mitigated the lending contraction primarily in countries where banking systems entered the crisis with higher capital buffer requirements. At the bank level, the effects of the CCyB release were strongest among banks with limited capital headroom, reducing interest rates but tightening maturity terms. These findings highlight that the effectiveness of countercyclical macroprudential policy depends on both system-level capital capacity and bank-level constraints.
papers.reason: Provides empirical evidence on how macroprudential capital buffers and countercyclical releases affect European bank lending conditions and corporate financing costs.

papers.title: Striking a Bargain: Narrative Identification of Wage Bargaining Shocks
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Wage markup shocks, an important driver of business cycles, are hard to pin down. We quantify the importance of exogenous variation in wage bargaining power, one source of those shocks, from German minimum wage introduction episodes and strikes. This disciplines the impulse responses of unemployment and output, and sharpens inference for other variables, which behave consistently with predictions from search‐and‐matching models. We find that wage bargaining shocks meaningfully contribute to aggregate fluctuations in unemployment and inflation, exhibit substantial pass‐through to prices, and imply plausible dynamics for the vacancy rate, firms' profits, and the labor share.
papers.reason: Quantifies the macroeconomic impact of wage bargaining shocks using German institutional data, offering clear implications for inflation pass-through.

papers.title: Subjective Models of the Macroeconomy and the Transmission of Monetary Policy
papers.abstract: Standard macroeconomic theories assume that representative or heterogeneous agents share a common model of how the economy operates.Yet evidence shows that households hold heterogeneous subjective models---distinct beliefs about how macroeconomic variables interact.As a result, identical shocks or policies may elicit different responses from otherwise similar households.We test this hypothesis by measuring subjective models and investigating their role in the transmission of monetary policy to consumption embedding randomized controlled experiment in a large-scale, multi-country survey.Consumers who believe that monetary tightening primarily operates through its effects on borrowing or savings rates plan to reduce consumption more in response to randomly assigned rate increase scenarios.By contrast, those who think about inflation or general equilibrium effects adjust consumption less.These differences are not explained by demographics, financial characteristics, including mortgage holdings and mortgage type, or country-level factors.Households' actual consumption responses to endogenous policy-rate changes exhibit broadly similar patterns.Our findings stress that heterogeneity in subjective models is an overlooked determinant of monetary policy transmission.
papers.reason: Demonstrates that household subjective macroeconomic models significantly influence consumption responses to monetary policy changes, providing a novel perspective on transmission.

papers.title: What is the Impact of a Major Unconventional Monetary Policy Intervention?
papers.abstract: How does the credible announcement of an unconventional monetary policy intervention affect bank lending standards during crises? We use a major central bank announcement, the "whatever it takes" speech of the European Central Bank President that boosted the capital of banks, as a natural experiment. We compare changes in lending standards of subsidiaries of euro area versus other banks in a third country, Mexico. The speech reversed a prior trend of euro area banks augmenting their risk taking via loan growth, lending rates, and credit risk. Our findings show that policies that amount to capitalization can reduce risk-taking in times of stress, adding a new dimension to the bank capital channel.
papers.reason: Uses a major ECB communication event to study bank lending standards of euro area bank subsidiaries in Mexico, highlighting international bank capital channels during stress.

papers.title: Do macro-financial conditions amplify shocks in banking system vulnerability?
papers.abstract: Can macro-financial conditions amplify adverse shocks originating in the banking system? We argue that when vulnerability in the banking system increases, the extent to which financial intermediation and the macroeconomy are adversely affected is likely to depend on whether banks are operating in normal times or under more challenging conditions. Using a Bayesian Panel Threshold VAR, data on euro area countries and a high-frequency, forward-looking measure of the banking system’s vulnerability to market-based equity losses, we show that nonlinearities matter. When the banking system is already in distress, lending and economic activity contract more severely following a further increase in banks’ vulnerability. Similarly, low interest rates, typically associated with low bank margins and profitability, correspond to larger declines in lending. In both environments, corporate lending contracts more than mortgage lending, a finding consistent with de-risking. The state of the business cycle, though, does not alter shock propagation to the same extent. Our findings suggest that it is particularly important for macroprudential policies to preserve banks’ resilience in times of stress, characterized by elevated banking system vulnerability and low interest rates.
papers.reason: Directly informs bank resilience, credit growth dynamics, and macroprudential policy in the euro area using bank-level and macroeconomic data.

papers.title: Causal Analysis for Time Series Foundation Models
papers.abstract: Transitioning from bespoke time series models towards time series foundation models changes the relationship of model and application from one-to-one to one-to-many. This shift introduces concentration risk as many, potentially high-risk, forecasting applications are exposed to the same biases and failure modes of a single time series foundation model. At the same time, this centralization allows for economies of scale in model development and validation. In this study we investigate how biases and failure modes of time series foundation models can be identified before deployment. We propose a causal analysis framework to investigate the ability of a time series foundation model to preserve time series patterns. To achieve this, we intervene on parameterized synthetic time series generators and measure the corresponding change in model output under ceteris paribus conditions. We apply our causal analysis framework to Chronos-2 and TimesFM-2.5 and test them across six distinct time series patterns. We find safe configurations for trend and harmonic oscillation patterns. The results also indicate a bias in both models towards overestimating persistence, sudden failures for both models against the regime switch pattern and failure for TimesFM-2.5 against the energy-release pattern. Our review of the original works for both models indicates that the findings might be explained by the data used for pretraining. We conclude our study with suggestions for further model development, recommendations for application-specific model selection, and a discussion of limitations and further research directions.
papers.reason: Examines methodologies and biases of time series foundation models, offering indirect technical relevance for forecasting infrastructure.

papers.title: House hunting high and low: Constructing a Housing Search Index for Portugal
papers.abstract: In this paper, we build a Housing Search Index (HSI) based on Google searches made within Portugal that are related to the house-buying process. This index is constructed as the first principal component of a series of search volumes related to house buying, and it is used as a predictor of house price changes. We find that the HSI contains substantial in and out-of-sample predictive information for short-term house price changes, especially in comparison to other predictors usually applied in this literature. The model also suggests that supply variables are not as strong indicators as the HSI. Furthermore, we show that foreign demand, as measured through Google search-based foreign HSIs, plays an important role in explaining Portuguese house price growth rates.
papers.reason: The paper constructs a Google search-based housing index for Portugal that predicts short-term house price changes, offering practical tools for regional real estate and mortgage market analysis.

papers.title: Smart Compaction: Predicting Compaction Utility from Lakehouse Table Metadata
papers.abstract: Open lakehouse table formats accumulate small data files over time, which degrades query performance. Deciding when compaction is worthwhile remains threshold-driven, but which metadata features actually determine compaction utility is not well understood. We present an open simulation framework that generates 2,376 Apache Iceberg tables spanning three orders of magnitude in file size, extracts 17 metadata features from manifest files without reading data, and trains XGBoost to predict the continuous file-reduction ratio (R2 = 0.998, RMSE= 0.013). The binary compaction decision turns out to be trivially separable by a single partition-level threshold max_files_per_partition> 4, requiring no learned model. Cross-schema validation on 96 TPC-H tables confirms generalisation without retraining (R2 = 0.976). A query benchmark reveals that compaction benefits metadata-heavy queries but can slow full-scan aggregations by reducing task parallelism. All code and data are publicly available.
papers.reason: This is a computer science and database engineering study on data file compaction in cloud lakehouses with no macroeconomic or market implications.

papers.abstract: This replication package reproduces the empirical analysis presented in Debt Sustainability as a Nominal Reconciliation Problem.

papers.title: The impact of environmental regulation on clean innovation: Are there crowding out effects?
papers.abstract: We examine how environmental regulation influences innovation, and which policy instruments most effectively stimulate technological development across 15 countries and 3 million firms. Employing panel local projections, we go beyond immediate impact and estimate effects of regulatory changes on patenting over a five-year horizon. To address gaps in emissions reporting, we estimate firm-level greenhouse gas emissions by a machine learning approach, which serve as a proxy for regulatory exposure. At the country level, stricter emission regulation shows little impact on overall environmental technology innovation. At the firm level, however, tighter policies spur innovation in climate change–mitigating technologies, without evidence of crowding out other forms of innovation. These effects are strongest for clean energy technologies, particularly among high polluters in energy-intensive sectors. Policy design plays a critical role: increases in the stringency of technology support and non-market-based instruments significantly boost clean technology patenting, whereas we find no robust effect of market-based instruments. This also holds specifically for clean energy technology patenting.
papers.reason: Evaluates how environmental regulations and policy instruments impact firm-level clean innovation across 15 countries, informing climate policy and industrial credit views.

papers.abstract: Maruyama, Toshitaka, and Tomohide Mineyama. Cyclicality and Asymmetry of the User Cost of Labor.
