papers.title: Conduct of Monetary Policy under Housing Market Imbalances
papers.abstract: Canadian housing imbalances have elevated shelter inflation as a driver of CPI, fueled by high house prices, mortgage costs, rents, supply constraints, and leverage. This note uses a model with housing supply and extrapolative expectations to assess whether monetary policy should incorporate or look through shelter inflation under demand and supply shocks.
papers.reason: Evaluates how monetary policy should respond to shelter inflation driven by housing imbalances, directly informing interest rate policy debates.

papers.title: Ownership, Diversity and the Effectiveness of Government‐backed Financial Support during a Systemic Crisis: Evidence from One Million UK SMEs
papers.abstract: Abstract Using proprietary data on over one million UK Small and Medium‐Sized Enterprises (SMEs) from 2017 to 2024, we examine how ownership composition and director diversity condition the impact of government‐backed Covid‐19 loan programmes on normal (non‐Covid) loan default outcomes. Building on the Behavioural Theory of the Firm and the Attention‐Based View, we develop Attention‐Based Governance (ABG) as a conceptual lens for explaining how SMEs deploy government‐backed slack during systemic crises. Our results show that SMEs with multiple owners from the same family are more effective than single‐owner SMEs in managing Covid support, indicating stronger internal collective oversight and discipline. Furthermore, SMEs with domestic institutional owners and female directors exhibit stronger capability and discipline, while those with foreign institutional owners or foreign directors display higher default risk on normal loans. Additional analysis reveals that foreign‐owned firms are least likely to default on the government‐backed Covid loans themselves. This finding reflects the selective allocation of managerial attention towards highly visible, publicly guaranteed debt to protect reputational capital with global stakeholders. Overall, our study shows how ownership composition and director diversity direct managerial attention and determine whether public funding leads to stronger financial resilience or heightened default risk at the firm level.
papers.reason: Examines UK SME loan defaults and governance factors during government support programmes, offering micro-level insights with indirect relevance for corporate credit assessment.

papers.title: Replication package for: The Macroeconomics of Wage Rigidity and Job Separations
papers.abstract: Blanco, Andrés, Andrés Drenik, Christian Moser, and Emilio Zaratiegui. 2026. "The Macroeconomics of Wage Rigidity and Job Separations." Review of Economic Studies, forthcoming (MS 36635). This package contains the code and data needed to reproduce every table and figure in the paper, using Stata to build the wage-change moments, Julia to estimate and simulate the model, and MATLAB to produce the figures.
papers.reason: Provides a replication package and code for a forthcoming academic study on wage rigidity and job separations, with no direct new market commentary.

papers.title: Do women comply more than men? Experimental evidence from a general population sample
papers.abstract: Women are typically perceived as more compliant than men; however, the literature provides inconclusive evidence. Using a novel experimental design comprising two complementary experiments, we test this claim in online samples representative of the German adult population. The first experiment (N = 1600) features a probabilistic social dilemma game (PDG) in which participants can increase their individual payoff at the expense of exposing themselves and their group to probabilistic losses. In two treatment conditions, they receive either a recommendation on socially optimal behavior or the same recommendation plus information on weakly non-compliant peer behavior. We find that the recommendation strongly affects behavior, but more so for women than for men. The welfare improvement is substantial. Information on the non-compliant behavior of others erodes compliance with recommendation but does not induce significantly different responses in men and women. In the second experiment (N = 522), we elicit empirical and normative expectations about behavior in the PDG with a behavioral recommendation, in order to study the role of norms in adhering to it. While men and women are expected to hold similar normative beliefs, men are expected to follow the recommendation less often, suggesting that compliance is a (strong) female social norm.
papers.reason: Experimental evidence on gender differences in compliance has little direct application to financial markets or macroeconomic forecasting.

papers.title: Structural forecast analysis
papers.abstract: Summary: This paper shows how the structural representation of a vector autoregressive model can support forecast analysis. We offer a unified framework that formalizes how the structural form of the model can help form a narrative for two key statistics in real-time vector autoregressive forecasting: the forecast errors at the outturn of the data, and the consequent revisions of the forecast. We conduct an exercise on the United Kingdom, focusing on the inflation surge that started in 2022. We show that revisions to the inflation forecast were driven not only by contractionary supply-side shocks, but also by a mix of expansionary demand-side shocks, with an important role played by revised past shocks. However, we find that the role of demand shocks was subsequently revised downwards as new data vintages become available.
papers.reason: The paper provides a structural VAR framework to analyze UK inflation forecast errors and revisions, offering insights relevant for rates and inflation strategists.

papers.title: The Labor Market Costs of Job Displacement by Migrant Status
papers.abstract: Abstract This paper examines the differential impact of job displacement on migrants and natives. Using administrative data for Germany from 1997–2016, we identify mass layoffs and estimate the trajectory of earnings and employment of observationally similar migrants and natives displaced from the same establishment. Despite similar pre-layoff careers, migrants’ earnings losses are about 23% larger in the first five years after displacement. This gap arises from both lower re-employment probabilities and post-layoff wages and is not driven by selective return migration. Key mechanisms include sorting into lower-quality firms and relying on lower-quality coworker networks during job search.
papers.reason: Examines job displacement costs for migrants versus natives using administrative German data, offering granular insights relevant to wage dynamics and structural labour market trends.

papers.title: Assessing risk: a toolkit for measuring regional supply-chain exposure to global shocks
papers.abstract: Abstract This article sheds light on the complexities of global supply chains’ (GSCs) subnational dimensions, including how international shocks propagate spatially. It develops a systematic approach or toolkit for analyzing how global shocks affect the regional distribution of GSCs. Using the toolkit, it derives a family of GSC indicators that distinguish between import- and export-side exposure, direct (face-value) and indirect (hidden exposure) linkages, and gross versus value-added flows. The article then applies the indicators to multiregional input–output data to highlight how global shocks propagate unevenly across regions and how impacts vary with the nature of the shock and a region’s type of exposure.
papers.reason: Develops a methodology for measuring regional exposure to global supply chain shocks, offering indirect insights for sectoral and regional risk assessments.

papers.title: Delivering on the G20 Roadmap: Unlocking collaboration and innovation in cross-border payments
papers.abstract: Improving cross-border payments remains a global priority. Significant progress has been made under the G20 Roadmap, with notable achievements such as the adoption of ISO 20022 and policy advancements led by international bodies like the Financial Stability Board (FSB), the Committee on Payments and Market Infrastructures, and the Financial Action Task Force. However, challenges persist, and bridging the gap between aspirations and outcomes will require strengthened collaboration between the public and private sectors. Geopolitical shifts and digital innovations are reshaping the financial landscape, demanding adaptive and forward-looking solutions. Achieving the Roadmap’s goals will depend on sustained commitment and coordinated efforts to develop long-term strategies that address structural barriers, with the FSB playing a key role in driving this progress. This article is also included in the Business & Management Collection which can be accessed at http://hstalks.com/business.
papers.reason: Discusses high-level G20 roadmap progress and public-private collaboration for cross-border payments without specific quantitative market conclusions.

papers.title: Optimal monetary and exchange rate frameworks for commodity-exposed economies
papers.abstract: We show that the optimal monetary and exchange rate frameworks depend critically on the economy’s commodity exposure. We develop a flexible but tractable model economy with commodity exports and imports, in which international financial conditions depend on the commodity cycle. Stabilizing domestic prices is optimal for commodity exporters, in line with standard open-economy policy prescriptions. But when economies import commodities as production inputs, optimal policy largely ‘looks through’ their direct and indirect effects on domestic prices. In emerging economies, where financial conditions are closely related to commodity cycles, trade-offs are starker and limited credibility may make implementing optimal policy challenging.
papers.reason: The study models optimal monetary and exchange rate policies for commodity-exposed economies based on international financial conditions.

papers.title: Spatial productivity disparities in Great Britain
papers.abstract: We study productivity disparities across metropolitan and non‐metropolitan areas in Great Britain. Spatial disparities in productivity are large and persistent. Using a development accounting framework, we show that differences in area size and in the spatial distribution of human and business capital are key explanatory factors. A combination of area size and human capital explains 30% of the productivity variance, increasing to 43–57% once we add measures of business capital stocks. Applying our framework to a case study of Greater Manchester, we show that large increases in both types of capital are needed to narrow productivity disparities with London, illustrating the scale of the challenge for policies aimed at reducing spatial inequality.
papers.reason: The research decomposes regional productivity disparities in Great Britain, providing useful structural insights for UK fiscal policy and regional development but limited immediate market application.

papers.title: The role of gasoline price expectations in transmitting gasoline price shocks to inflation and real activity
papers.abstract: This paper argues that gasoline price fluctuations affect inflation through changes in consumer expectations about future energy costs. More precisely, we use data from the US Michigan Survey of Consumers and estimate a Structural VAR model to show that long-run gasoline price expectations are an important transmission channel through which gasoline price shocks are propagated to both inflation and real economic activity. These findings suggest that monitoring consumer energy price expectations offers policymakers an early warning signal for inflationary pressure, which is a useful tool in addition to broader inflation anchoring. As energy market volatility intensifies in an era of geopolitical uncertainty and green transition, understanding this channel becomes increasingly important for monetary policy.
papers.reason: Demonstrates that consumer gasoline price expectations transmit energy shocks to US inflation and real activity, providing a useful indicator for monetary policy.

papers.title: Offshoring and voting patterns in the US
papers.abstract: This paper studies the impact of offshoring by US firms on voting patterns in the US. Using county-level voting data combined with industry-level offshoring data, we ask whether an increase in employment at foreign affiliates of US multinationals in vertically oriented industries is associated with an increase in the vote share for the incumbent party candidate in Presidential, House, and Senate elections. We find that offshoring leads to an increase in the incumbent vote share for counties with more educated workers, and a decrease for counties with higher shares of workers in the manufacturing sector and in occupations that are more easily relocated abroad. These results are consistent with the labor market literature on offshoring, which shows that offshoring has heterogeneous effects on workers’ employment based on skill and occupational tasks. This suggests that voters respond to the economic effects of offshoring by rewarding or punishing incumbent party candidates.
papers.reason: The study links US firm offshoring to domestic voting patterns across counties, providing indirect political economy context for trade and labor market adjustments.

papers.title: BoC–BoE Sovereign Default Database: What’s new in 2026?
papers.abstract: Since 2014, the Bank of Canada (BoC) has maintained a comprehensive database of sovereign defaults to systematically measure and aggregate the nominal value of the different types of sovereign government debt in default. The database draws on published datasets compiled by various public and private sector sources. It combines elements of these sources with new information to develop comprehensive estimates of stocks of government obligations in default. These include bonds and other marketable securities, as well as bank loans and official loans, valued in US dollars, for the years 1960 to 2025, on both a country-by-country and a global basis. We consider debt to be in distress—and effectively in default—when an interruption in scheduled debt service occurs, a sovereign seeks to renegotiate the existing contract terms of any of its obligations or a combination of both. Such restructurings can include writing down the principal, reducing the interest rate or extending maturities. Typically, they also involve creditors suffering a loss in net present value. Once restructured, the debt is reclassified as performing and no longer considered to be in default. Official creditors include the International Monetary Fund (IMF), the World Bank, other multilateral development banks, Paris Club creditors, non-Paris Club G20 creditors (notably China, India and South Africa) and other government development agencies. Private creditors are external bondholders, banks and suppliers. The database is posted on the BoC’s website and is updated annually in partnership with the Bank of England (BoE). Regular updates of the BoC–BoE database are useful to researchers analyzing the economic and financial effects of individual sovereign defaults and, importantly, the impacts on global financial stability from episodes involving multiple sovereign defaults. In this paper, we: highlight developments in sovereign debt defaults in 2025, including details on the estimated 14% decrease in the US-dollar value of sovereign debt in default from 2024 levels update key insights regarding the number, size and types of defaults give a historical overview of debt defaults and their persistence in heavily indebted, low-income sovereigns examine the shift in bilateral official sovereign lending from Paris Club lenders toward China1 update our estimates of stocks of domestic arrears, valued in US dollars The 2026 edition of the database, as well as related research, contains several enhancements, including: revisions to country and aggregate default data for 1960 to 2025, which include: new data on domestic arrears by country and globally, most comprehensively for the years 1990 to 2025 an illustration (Figure 1) showing debt in default across different regions a figure showing the proportion of sovereign debt in default and debt as a share of gross domestic product (GDP) by country updates to documents containing the methodology, appendix and references
papers.reason: The updated multi-decade sovereign default database provides essential empirical grounding for assessing sovereign credit risk and debt restructurings.

papers.title: Canada’s Cross-Border Carry Trade
papers.abstract: Canada has been spending more than its national income for much of the period since the Global Financial Crisis, relying for this on net financing from rest of the world. Yet Canada’s foreign asset position has grown substantially than its foreign liabilities despite these deficits. This improvement reflects favorable changes in asset prices and exchange rates. From 1990Q1 to 2026Q2, estimated cumulative valuation gains were about 3 times as large as the cumulative current-account deficit. These gains also reflect a favorable portfolio composition. Canada increasingly holds foreign equity and direct investment, much of it denominated in U.S. dollars, while issuing relatively safer Canadian-dollar debt. Hence, higher returns on foreign equities, together with an appreciation of the U.S. dollar, raised the value of Canada’s net foreign assets. Larger gross positions over time amplified these valuation effects. Overall, valuation gains have relaxed the current-account adjustment needed to stabilize Canada’s external position, permitting a higher level of national expenditure than would otherwise have been feasible.
papers.reason: Analyzes how foreign asset valuation gains and currency shifts sustain current account deficits in Canada, relevant for sovereign credit and FX risk assessments.

papers.title: How Costly Are Cross-Border Payments for Firms?
papers.abstract: How costly are cross-border payments for firms? Using proprietary FXC Intelligence data on quoted prices for Canadian business-to-business cross-border payments, this note documents three empirical facts. First, cross-border payment costs for firms are costly: banks charge senders a total margin of around 2–3.5% of transaction value, with foreign exchange margins accounting for the majority of these costs relative to transaction fees. Second, payment costs for vehicle currencies tend to be lower. Third, for the same corridor and transfer amount, prices differ substantially across banks, and the size of this dispersion is corridor-specific.
papers.reason: Quantifies corporate cross-border payment and FX margins for Canadian firms, providing useful micro-level pricing data for wholesale banking and payments desks.

papers.title: Auction Timing Under Limited Information: Evidence from Sovereign Bond Auctions
papers.abstract: This paper examines how auction timing may affect sovereign issuance outcomes through its interaction with market volatility. Using Canada as a case study, it shows that: (1) higher same-day bond market volatility is associated with larger auction tails, indicating weaker demand conditions; and (2) monetary policy announcements and certain macroeconomic data releases are systematically associated with higher same-day volatility. Together, these findings identify one observable channel linking information available at the schedule-setting horizon to auction outcomes. Within issuance frameworks that prioritize market predictability and operate under limited information sets, the results suggest that auction timing may influence outcomes at the margin.
papers.reason: Demonstrates that same-day market volatility and macro announcements widen sovereign auction tails, offering actionable insights for rates trading and issuance timing.

papers.title: The Distributional Consequences of Commodity Booms
papers.abstract: This paper examines the response of income inequality to commodity price shocks and identifies the underlying mechanisms at play. I provide novel cross-country evidence from commodity-exporting nations, showing that positive commodity price shocks reduce labor income inequality between skilled and unskilled workers. This reduction in inequality is primarily driven by a fall in the skill premium, arising from the expansion of unskilled-labor-intensive sectors, such as construction, which grow more rapidly than skilled-labor-intensive ones, such as services. To interpret these results, I develop a quantitative multisector small-open-economy model that incorporates sectoral heterogeneity in both skilled-labor intensity and sensitivity to commodity price shocks. I use the model as a laboratory to explore the distributional impacts of various policy responses to commodity windfalls, demonstrating how saving or spending these gains can either reinforce or moderate the reduction in inequality. This analysis provides new insights into the broader economic and social impacts of commodity price shocks in emerging markets.
papers.reason: Examines how positive commodity price shocks reduce skill premia in emerging market economies, providing macro-structural context for commodity-exporting sovereign credits.

papers.title: Beyond "Looking Through": Monetary Policy Responses and Communication Under Supply-Driven Inflation
papers.abstract: Using a controlled macroeconomic experiment, we compare monetary policy rules that differ in how much they look through inflation: a Lean-Against policy that responds strongly to inflation and a Look-Through policy that responds less strongly. We combine each rule with communication protocols that vary the information the central bank releases about its policy response: restricted qualitative information, detailed quantitative information, and detailed quantitative information combined with inflation and output projections. Midway through each session, we raise the persistence of the cost-push shock. Looking through large, persistent shocks raises and prolongs inflation and increases the risk that inflation expectations unanchoring, while responding with tighter policy curbs inflation sooner. Communication matters mainly through projections. Adding detailed quantitative information to qualitative statements has little effect on output gaps, inflation, expectations or forecast errors. Communicating projections reduces inflation and output losses, anchors inflation expectations and lowers forecast errors. Under Look-Through, projections anchor inflation expectations and reduce inflation after the increase in supply shock persistence. Looking through supply-shock-induced inflation is only advisable when the central bank can communicate credible and focal projections to guide expectations.
papers.reason: Compares monetary policy rules and communication strategies under persistent supply shocks, offering direct insights for central bank reaction functions and inflation pricing.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence and Financial Tail Risks
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has a double-edged relationship with financial stability: it may improve efficiency and risk management, while also creating new vulnerabilities and amplification channels. This paper studies whether market-perceived exposure to AI is reflected in the tails of financial-sector returns, and whether this relationship depends on macroeconomic conditions. We develop a framework that decomposes financial-sector tail outcomes across contemporaneous AI and macroeconomic scenarios, and identifies whether the AI-related episodes are primarily associated with extreme gains or losses. Using daily equity returns for financial sectors in Canada, the United States, Europe, the United Kingdom, and China, we document substantial heterogeneity. Financial-sector-specific scenarios dominate tail outcomes across markets, while the contribution of AI-related scenarios to return asymmetry differs substantially across countries. AI-sector scenarios contribute to downside asymmetry in Europe, China, and especially the United Kingdom, but make only a limited contribution in Canada and have the smallest tail weights in the United States. China is the only market exhibiting positive average skewness, driven by the financial and systemic scenarios rather than by AI-related outcomes. Overall, AI-related market movements are neither uniformly stabilizing nor destabilizing; their financial-stability interpretation depends on the market considered and on whether AI-sector tail events occur in isolation or jointly with broader macroeconomic movements.
papers.reason: Evaluates how market-perceived AI exposure affects financial-sector return distributions across major global economies, informing banking sector risk and equity research.

papers.title: Demand roars, supply whispers: Monetary policy and housing in Canada
papers.abstract: We examine the effects of monetary policy shocks on the Canadian housing market. Using high-frequency surprises around fixed announcement dates as an instrument in a Bayesian VAR, we estimate the responses of house prices, housing starts, building permits, resales, inventories, and mortgage origination to a contractionary monetary policy shock. An increase in the policy rate leads to a substantial and persistent decline in average house prices. Housing starts and building permits fall, but their implied effects on the future housing stock are both slow and modest. Interpreted through the lens of market equilibrium, these results are most consistent with a stronger response of housing demand than housing supply. Mortgage origination provides additional evidence in support of this interpretation.
papers.reason: The paper provides direct empirical estimates of monetary policy transmission to house prices and mortgage origination, informing rates and housing sector strategies.

papers.title: Replication Package for Offshoring and Voting Patterns in the US
papers.abstract: Replication package for Offshoring and Voting Patterns in the US by Anna Maria Mayda, Lindsay Oldenski, and Walter Steingress

papers.title: Forecasting oil prices: What works best and when
papers.abstract: Oil price forecasts help central banks assess risks to inflation and economic activity. Forecasters often rely on the latest price of oil, on futures markets or on economic models. The best approach depends on how far ahead forecasters are looking and whether they need only a forecast or also an explanation of what’s behind it.
papers.reason: Discusses methodologies for forecasting oil prices, which inform central bank inflation assessments and commodity trading strategies.

papers.title: Money Creation for Crypto Space: Stablecoins or Central Bank Digital Currencies?
papers.abstract: Stablecoins are the current go-to digital money to settle transactions on the blockchain. We explore the implications of introducing competing tokenized public digital monies (i.e., tokenized central bank digital currencies (CBDCs)). When they pay a moderate interest rate and guarantee users’ anonymity, tokenized CBDCs crowd out stablecoins. However, when they pay a high interest rate and have low anonymity features, stablecoin issuers could use tokenized CBDCs as collateral, promoting the creation of stablecoins. We identify conditions under which introducing a CBDC to compete with stablecoins in the crypto sector would be socially optimal. This paper was accepted by Will Cong for the Virtual Special Issue on Digital Finance. Funding: Support from Swiss National Science Foundation (SNSF) [Grant 100018 219835].
papers.reason: Analyzes conditions under which tokenized central bank digital currencies crowd out or support stablecoins in the blockchain ecosystem.

papers.title: The Production Network Amplification of Retaliatory Tariffs
papers.abstract: We develop a framework to quantify how tariff changes on imported goods affect sectoral and aggregate consumption prices through direct and production-network channels. Using Canada's input-output matrix and administrative firm-good import data for the universe of Canadian firms, we estimate price elasticities for tariffs on U.S.-imported goods. Tariffs on machinery and equipment and transport equipment generate the largest effects on final prices, reflecting their widespread use as intermediate inputs. On average, two-thirds of the total price response stems from higher intermediate input costs passing through domestic supply chains. Applying the framework to Canada's 2025 counter-tariffs, we estimate consumption price increases of 1.56 and 0.72 percentage points for the pre- and post-September 2025 phases, respectively; alternative packages of equal import value could reduce aggregate price effects by three to seven times. A hypothetical CUSMA breakdown reverting to MFN tariffs would raise final-good prices by 0.64 percentage points.
papers.reason: Quantifies the impact of retaliatory tariffs on Canadian consumer prices through input-output linkages, informing trade policy and inflation outlooks.

papers.title: How Do Import Tariffs Affect Aggregate Prices? Theory and Evidence from Canada
papers.abstract: By how much do import tariffs raise aggregate prices? We develop a simple decomposition that separates the aggregate price effect of a tariff into three channels—cost pass-through, markup adjustments, and consumer substitution across varieties—and calibrate an oligopolistic competition model with endogenous markups to firm-level market shares for Canadian domestic producers, U.S. exporters, and rest-of-world suppliers. A 25% counter-tariff on U.S. imports raises Canada's aggregate price index by 0.66—well below the 1.25% that direct cost pass-through alone would predict. The dominant offsetting force is consumer substitution toward non-U.S. varieties, which reduces the price effect by 0.47 percentage points; markup adjustments, holding fixed pre-tariff market shares, contribute a further 0.26 percentage point decrease. The gap between cost pass-through and the true price effect widens sharply with the tariff rate: at a 50% tariff, cost pass-through alone predicts more than twice the true price effect.
papers.reason: Provides a quantitative model showing how consumer substitution and markups mitigate tariff passthrough on aggregate price indices in Canada.

papers.title: Stress in the Press or Stress in the Market: A New Measure of Perceived Financial Stress
papers.abstract: We develop a news-based measure of perceived financial stress for Canada using more than 900,000 business and economic news articles from 1977 to 2026. Using a data-driven keyword discovery algorithm, we construct an interpretable News-based Stress Index (NSI) that tracks major stress episodes and captures periods when concerns about financial risks intensify despite limited market disruption. Using linear and quantile-augmented VARs, we show that news shocks orthogonal to financial shocks primarily reduce unsecured consumer credit by shifting its entire distribution, whereas market-based financial shocks primarily worsen downside risks to both credit and real activity. This highlights perceived financial stress as a distinct transmission channel operating through household precautionary behavior.
papers.reason: Constructs a news-based financial stress index for Canada and demonstrates its specific transmission channels to consumer credit and real activity.

papers.title: Living in a Ghost Town: The Geography of Depopulation and Aging
papers.abstract: How do depopulation and population aging evolve differently across regions within a country, and what are their implications for aggregate economic activity and regional inequality?Using spatially disaggregated data from Japan over the past several decades, we show that rural areas have experienced significantly faster depopulation and aging than urban areas, driven by low fertility and sustained out-migration of young cohorts.Regions undergoing these trends face declining local amenities and rising per-capita public service costs.To study the future evolution and economic consequences of these dynamics, we develop and calibrate a dynamic life-cycle spatial general equilibrium model.The model predicts widening geographic disparities in depopulation, aging, and economic activity in the coming centuries.While subsidies to declining regions can lower regional inequality, they come at the cost of lower aggregate efficiency and higher public service expenditures.
papers.reason: Analysis of regional depopulation and aging using Japanese data highlights long-term structural shifts in public expenditures and regional economic disparities.

papers.title: Sector-based producer price indexes: New measures of producer price pressures in Canada
papers.abstract: Producer price indexes measure changes in the prices that producers receive for their outputs or that they pay for their inputs. Statistics Canada publishes a range of producer price indexes for specific products and industries. For the first time, these series have been combined into a small set of broad sectoral measures.
papers.reason: Introduces new sectoral producer price indexes for Canada, offering improved data granularity for inflation monitoring but limited direct analytical conclusions.

papers.title: Prima: The Bank of Canada’s New Projection and Policy-Analysis Model—An Overview
papers.abstract: Prima is the Bank of Canada’s new model for projection and policy analysis. It builds on the economic foundations of earlier Bank models, adding detail on how sectoral pressures affect production costs and their pass-through to consumer prices.
papers.reason: Outlines the Bank of Canada's new projection and policy-analysis model, providing insights into how sectoral cost pressures pass through to consumer prices.

papers.title: Simultaneous inference in possibly incomplete multivariate regressions with application to asset pricing
papers.abstract: This paper presents finite-sample tests and confidence procedures for a multivariate linear regression system with cross-dependent possibly non-Gaussian disturbances, allowing for potentially missing explanatory variables. We consider a wide class of multivariate statis- tics based on the roots of a determinantal equation involving restricted and unrestricted least squares residuals. We characterize the exact distribution of these roots and identify important pivotal cases. General conditions for asymptotic validity are also given. To deal with missing explanatory variables, we introduce an identifiable ex-post parameter which embeds the impact of left-out variables, and show that usual tests remain valid from a conservative perspective. We derive simultaneous confidence bands for a vector (as well as linear combinations) of regression coefficients. The results are applied to asset pricing, with focus on risk-return analysis. We revisit the distinction between the alpha (risk-adjusted outperformance) and beta (risk component) of returns, from our ex-post parametrization perspective. Empirically, we analyze the risk-return profile of Catastrophe bond mutual funds.
papers.reason: Develops econometric tests for multivariate regressions and applies them to risk-return analysis and catastrophe bond mutual funds, relevant for quantitative asset pricing.

papers.title: What happens after Governing Council sets the policy interest rate: Inside the implementation framework that makes monetary policy work
papers.abstract: What happens after Governing Council sets the target for the policy interest rate? Setting the target rate is the most visible part of monetary policy, but it is only the first step in transmitting the rate decision to the Canadian economy. This paper explains how the Bank of Canada uses its monetary policy implementation framework (MPI) to ensure that the rate decision is reflected in financial markets by keeping short-term interest rates close to the target policy rate.
papers.reason: Describes the mechanics of the Bank of Canada's implementation framework for keeping short-term rates near the target.

papers.title: Why asking rents have surged in Canada since 2021
papers.abstract: Renting has become significantly more expensive in Canada in recent years. Asking rents—those advertised for vacant units—rose sharply as demand grew faster than supply. As tenants move and sign new leases, changes in asking rents gradually spread to the average rents captured in the consumer price index.
papers.reason: Provides micro-level evidence on Canadian asking rents and their passthrough to consumer price index inflation.

papers.title: Code for "Markups and Inflation in Oligopolistic Markets: Evidence from Wholesale Price Data"
papers.abstract: Replication package for peer-reviewed article forthcoming in American Economic Journal: Macroeconomics. Paper published online Month XX, 20XX. When citing this dataset, please also cite the associated article. A sample Publication Citation is provided below.
papers.reason: This is solely a replication code package for an upcoming journal article without direct standalone analysis for immediate market positioning.

papers.title: The budget pressures faced by different households since 2020
papers.abstract: Although inflation has come down from pandemic highs, many households are still feeling the effects of higher prices. Between 2020 and 2025, younger and lower‑income households generally saw spending outpace income gains while older and higher-income households fared better. Together, these differing experiences meant income gains for the average household kept up with higher spending.
papers.reason: Provides granular evidence on household spending and income divergence across age and income brackets in Canada since 2020, offering indirect context for consumer credit and domestic demand.

papers.title: A Stochastic Nested Fixed Point Algorithm for Large-Scale BLP Estimation
papers.abstract: We develop a stochastic nested fixed point (SNFP) estimator for random coefficients logit demand models that updates model parameters using stochastic gradients and performs demand inversion one market at a time. Relative to the conventional nested fixed point (NFP) estimator, SNFP substantially reduces memory requirements and computational cost, making estimation feasible in very large datasets. We establish the large-$T$ (number of markets) asymptotic properties of the estimator under regularity conditions. We also characterize the effect of sharing one block of simulation draws across markets and show how to correct for it. Monte Carlo simulations show that the SNFP estimator achieves statistical accuracy comparable to the NFP estimator, and in our benchmark a single online pass estimates a model with 100 million markets in about 5.5 hours. An empirical application using scanner data further demonstrates the practical advantages of SNFP for large-scale demand estimation.
papers.reason: It presents a purely methodological algorithm for large-scale demand estimation, with no direct macro or market application.

papers.title: What volatility reveals
papers.abstract: This paper studies the financial-market transmission of the April 2025 U.S. tariff announcements, with a particular focus on the unusual combination of dollar depre ciation and rising long-term U.S. Treasury yields. We ask whether the market reac tion can be understood as the propagation of a single tariff-announcement shock or instead reflects the interaction of distinct macro-financial disturbances. To address this question, we exploit time-varying volatility and non-Gaussian excess kurtosis in structural shocks to recover macro-financial forces without imposing event-based restrictions or exclusion assumptions. Our results show that the initial market reaction is consistent with a conventional safe-haven shock, but this mechanism cannot account for the subsequent joint behaviour of exchange rates and long-term U.S. Treasury yields. Instead, different segments of financial markets are dominated by distinct orthogonal shocks associated with safe-haven demand, confidence in U.S. institutions, Treasury-market intermediation, and changes in the convenience value of dollar-denominated safe assets
papers.reason: The paper investigates the market transmission of U.S. tariff announcements and the joint behavior of dollar depreciation and long-term Treasury yields using structural volatility models.

analysis.summary: This paper examines financial market reactions to the April 2025 U.S. tariff announcements, focusing on the unusual combination of U.S. dollar depreciation and rising long-term U.S. Treasury yields. Using a VAR model identified through time-varying stochastic volatility and Student-t shock distributions on daily data from January 2008 to May 2025, the authors decompose market dynamics without event or exclusion restrictions. They find that while initial equity declines reflected a standard safe-haven shock, subsequent market movements were driven by distinct orthogonal disturbances: a U.S. institutional credibility shock that depreciated the dollar and raised yields, and a Treasury intermediation shock that impaired swap spreads.
key_takeaways: Traditional safe-haven shocks explain initial equity drops and VIX spikes during April 2025, but fail to account for persistent U.S. dollar depreciation and rising long-term Treasury yields.
The post-announcement dollar depreciation and yield increases were driven by a U.S. institutional credibility shock that repriced dollar assets and raised one-year inflation swap expectations.
Using daily data from 2008 to 2025, a separate Treasury market intermediation shock explains the narrowing of 10-year U.S. swap spreads and declines in Treasury convenience yields.
analysis.relevance: This paper informs FX, rates, and cross-asset strategists analyzing trade policy shocks and reserve-currency dynamics. It demonstrates that U.S. trade announcements do not mechanically induce traditional safe-haven inflows into the dollar and U.S. Treasuries. By isolating separate shocks to U.S. institutional credibility and Treasury market intermediation, strategists can better model scenarios where trade policy announcements weaken the dollar, push up U.S. long-term yields and term premia, and impair Treasury dealer balance-sheet capacity.
analysis.market_focus_rationale: The empirical study focuses entirely on advanced economy financial assets, analyzing U.S. Treasuries, the U.S. dollar, euro area government bond yields, and U.S. equity indexes.

papers.title: Beyond technocracy: Toward a holistic approach to central bank trust
papers.abstract: We examine public trust in the European Central Bank (ECB) and its correlates using survey data from the Bundesbank Online Panel of Households for Germany. Drawing on insights from political science and psychology, we move beyond technocracy and develop a more holistic account of central bank trust. We show that trust in the ECB is associated with both competence aspects, defined as effectiveness in maintaining price stability and reliance on rules, scientific analysis and data—and value aspects, particularly the integrity of senior policymakers, honest communication and broader societal concern. Respondents who report that competence matters more report significantly higher trust in the ECB. In contrast, those who place greater importance on values tend to express lower trust. Trust in the ECB is also strongly associated with trust in political institutions more generally and, to a lesser extent, interpersonal trust. Together, our findings offer a fresh perspective on trust in central banks, in which respondents report value-related considerations alongside competence. Integrity and transparent communication are already part of the ECB’s existing ethics and accountability framework, so placing weight on these considerations raises no question about its mandate.
papers.reason: Analyzes survey data on public trust in the ECB among German households, touching on institutional credibility rather than market pricing.

papers.title: Perspectives on Objectives and Design Principles in Offline Payments with Central Bank Digital Currency
papers.abstract: In this work, fundamental design principles for a central bank digital currency (CBDC) with offline functionality and corresponding countermeasures are discussed. We identify three major objectives relevant for core security and privacy properties of such CBDC proposals: (i) Access Control Security—protection of a user’s funds against unauthorized access by other users; (ii) Security against Depositor Misbehavior—preservation of the integrity of an environment (potentially the wallet) against misbehavior of its owner (for example, double-spending); (iii) Privacy by Design—ensuring privacy is embedded into the system architecture. Our central conclusion is based on the alignment of the objectives to concrete design elements as countermeasures; certain objectives and countermeasures have no or minimal interference with each other. A major consequence of our work is that the integrity of a user’s wallet and, accordingly, the mitigation of double-spending race attacks should be addressed through the adaptation and integration of secure hardware or functionally equivalent trusted execution mechanisms within a CBDC system. The developed framework is applied for the analysis of five academic proposals of payment systems.
papers.reason: Examines design principles and security requirements for offline central bank digital currencies, providing relevant technical analysis for monetary authorities and payments infrastructure.

papers.title: Khalil_Strobel_Capital_Reallocation_under_Climate_Policy_Uncertainty
papers.abstract: The files in this repository replicate the results of the Paper Capital Reallocation under Climate Policy Uncertainty by Makram Khalil (Deutsche Bundesbank) and Felix Strobel (Deutsche Bundesbank).

papers.title: Stress testing European banks’ transition risk and lending behavior
papers.abstract: This paper investigates whether supervisory climate stress tests change how euroarea banks price and allocate credit according to borrowers’ transition risk. We combine loan-level data from the Eurosystem’s AnaCredit database with a firmlevel measure of greenhouse-gas (GHG) intensity and compare banks subject to the ECB’s 2021-22 climate stress test with non-participating banks. A difference-indifferences-in-slopes design estimates whether the sensitivity of new-loan spreads to carbon intensity changed after the exercise. The average shift in this spread intensity relationship is small and statistically insignificant. However, decomposing the aggregate effect reveals economically meaningful and offsetting adjustments. Participating banks reallocate new credit away from more carbon-intensive incumbent borrowers, while applying more carbon-sensitive pricing to relationships that enter or exit their portfolios; for new borrowers, a one-standard-deviation increase in carbon intensity is associated with about 10 basis points higher spreads. By contrast, repricing within continuing bank-firm relationships remains limited. The effects are strongest among the most carbon-intensive firms, and participation in the more demanding bottom-up module does not generate a clearly additional response. Overall, climate stress tests appear to operate mainly through portfolio recomposition and extensive-margin pricing, consistent with an information-and supervisory-scrutiny channel rather than a broad repricing of existing loans
papers.reason: Evaluates how euro area supervisory climate stress tests affect bank credit allocation and pricing across carbon-intensive borrowers, directly informing bank lending behavior and credit risk.

papers.title: Earnings dynamics through boom, crisis, and recovery: Evidence from Greece
papers.abstract: This paper documents the evolution of labor earnings and earnings dynamics in Greece during 2002–2023 using administrative matched employer–employee data from the Greek social security system. The data span the expansion of the 2000s, the deep recession of 2009–2013, and the subsequent recovery. We show that earnings, volatility, and inequality closely tracked macroeconomic conditions. Real earnings rose during the pre-crisis expansion, declined sharply during the recession (particularly among lower earners) and only partially recovered afterward. Earnings volatility and downside risk increased substantially during the crisis, while inequality rose both in the cross-section and within cohorts. Workers entering the labor market during the recession experienced unusually weak initial earnings and persistently lower subsequent earnings. Using regional variation in unemployment rates, we show that weaker local labor-market conditions at entry are associated with lower early-career earnings.
papers.reason: Documents long-term earnings, volatility, and inequality trends through macroeconomic cycles in Greece, providing useful context for European labor-market health.

papers.title: On the empirical relevance of the exchange rate as a shock absorber at the zero lower bound
papers.abstract: The New Keynesian argument is that flexible exchange rate regimes cannot stabilize cyclical developments at the ZLB, as the real exchange rate appreciates in response to adverse demand shocks. We estimate the effects of a negative domestic demand shock on the real exchange rate for the euro area vis-à-vis the United States, Canada, and Japan by state-dependent sign-restricted local projection methods. We find a real depreciation when interest rates are not at the ZLB, but also when they are. The exchange rate can accommodate considerable variations in output, confirming its shock-absorbing capacity away and during ZLB episodes. The stabilizing role of the exchange rate is accompanied by a significant expansion of the ECB’s balance sheet at the ZLB, while it remained unaffected in the non-ZLB period.
papers.reason: Provides empirical evidence that the euro area real exchange rate acts as a shock absorber even at the zero lower bound, informing FX and monetary policy views.

papers.title: Monetary policy and mergers and acquisitions
papers.abstract: We analyze the effect of monetary policy on mergers and acquisitions (M&A) activity using transaction and balance sheet data of public U.S. companies. We provide causal evidence that contractionary monetary policy reduces M&A activity. The response is particularly pronounced among financially constrained and higher-marginal product of capital firms, causing a change in the composition of firms conducting M&A. This in turn reduces the efficiency at which capital is reallocated via M&A.
papers.reason: Demonstrates the causal impact of contractionary monetary policy on corporate M&A activity and capital reallocation efficiency using U.S. firm data.

papers.title: Welche Faktoren beeinflussen die Weitergabe von Leit- und Geldmarktzinsänderungen an Unternehmenskreditzinsen?
papers.abstract: Warum stieg der Zins für Unternehmenskredite während des jüngsten Straffungszyklus weniger stark an als die Leit- und Geldmarktzinsen? Bisherige Befunde, dass die Zinsweitergabe unvollständig ist, beruhen auf aggregierten Daten. Offen blieb daher, welche Faktoren auf der Einzelkreditebene eine Rolle spielen. Dies beleuchten wir in unserer Studie und zeigen: Neben der Weitergabe von Refinanzierungskosten war eine veränderte Bepreisung von Kreditmerkmalen zentral – weniger jedoch eine veränderte Zusammensetzung des Kreditgeschäfts.
papers.reason: Using micro-level bank data, the study examines how policy rate changes pass through to corporate lending rates, informing credit and banking analysis.

papers.title: Which factors influence the pass-through of changes in policy and money market rates to bank lending rates to firms?
papers.abstract: Why didn’t lending rates for bank lending to firms rise as much as policy and money market rates in the recent monetary tightening cycle? Earlier findings that interest rate pass-through is incomplete are based on aggregate data. The question of which factors are at play at the micro (credit) level is yet left unexplored. We pick up on this topic in our study. Our finding: the main factor, alongside the pass-through of funding costs, was a change in the pricing of credit characteristics, while compositional shifts in lending played a minor role
papers.reason: This is the English-language version of the Bundesbank study analyzing micro-level drivers of incomplete interest rate pass-through to corporate loans.

papers.title: What Volatility Reveals: Agnostic Identification of Exchange Rate and Treasury-Market Dynamics in Inconvenient Times
papers.abstract: This paper studies the financial-market transmission of the April 2025 U.S. tariff announcements, with a particular focus on the unusual combination of dollar depreciation and rising long-term U.S. Treasury yields. We ask whether the market reaction can be understood as the propagation of a single tariff-announcement shock or whether it instead reflects the interaction of distinct macro-financial disturbances. To address this question, we exploit time variation in the volatility and excess kurtosis of structural shocks to recover macro-financial forces without imposing event-based restrictions or exclusion assumptions. Our results show that the initial market reaction is consistent with a conventional safe-haven shock, but this mechanism cannot account for the subsequent joint behaviour of exchange rates and long-term U.S. Treasury yields. Instead, different segments of financial markets are dominated by distinct orthogonal shocks associated with safe-haven demand, confidence in U.S. institutions, Treasury-market intermediation and changes in the convenience value of dollar-denominated safe assets.
papers.reason: It analyzes the market transmission of U.S. tariff announcements and the joint behavior of the dollar and Treasury yields using volatility-based identification, directly informing FX and rates strategists.

papers.title: Macroeconomic effects of carbon-intensive energy price changes
papers.abstract: This paper presents a novel model comparison to examine the challenges posed by changes in carbon-intensive energy prices for monetary policy. The employed environmental mon etary models have a detailed multi-sector structure. The comparison assesses the effects of both a temporary and a permanent energy price increase with a particular focus on the euro area and the United States. Temporary and permanent price shocks are both inflationary. However, the inflationary impact of the permanent shock depends on the underlying model assumptions and monetary policy response. The analysis also estab lishes that these models share large commonalities in their quantitative and qualitative results, while also pointing out cross-country differences.
papers.reason: Evaluates how temporary and permanent carbon-intensive energy price shocks impact euro area and US inflation and monetary policy.

papers.title: Carbon pricing, trade and the natural rate
papers.abstract: Introducing carbon pricing increases production costs and reduces output, at least initially. Benefits from reduced emissions damage materialize only later. This affects households’ saving behavior and, thereby, the natural interest rate r∗. Using a dynamic, three-region environmental life-cycle model, we find that the effects on the natural interest rate and net foreign asset positions crucially depend on how governments recycle carbon revenues. If carbon revenues are paid back to all households in a lump-sum manner, saving declines, the natural rate increases permanently and the net foreign asset position of the carbon pricing-increasing country falls. The opposite holds if only the working-age population benefits from carbon revenues. The impact on exchange rates and trade flows depends on which regions introduce carbon pricing (and potential border adjustment mechanisms) as this ultimately drives relative price changes across the regions
papers.reason: Examines how carbon pricing and revenue recycling schemes affect the natural interest rate, net foreign assets, and trade flows.

papers.title: Nonlinear economic damages from compound heat and drought events
papers.abstract: Abstract Europe is increasingly exposed to heatwaves and droughts, yet their short-term, sector-specific economic impacts remain difficult to quantify in predictive frameworks. We develop climate-augmented models for regional real growth in per capita gross value added across 1117 EU regions over 2002–2022, combining standard economic indicators with high-frequency climate variables capturing heatwaves and multiple drought types across temporal horizons. Using mixed-frequency designs and machine learning (ML) approaches, Random Forest and XGBoost, we show that climate predictors improve predictive accuracy relative to linear benchmarks in the climate-sensitive agricultural sector. In contrast, other sectoral aggregations exhibit more limited gains, and climate-augmented specifications do not consistently outperform their economic-only counterparts. Heatwave indicators contribute robustly to predictive performance, while the importance of drought varies by sector. Simulations of an extreme compound heat-drought scenario using XGBoost suggest that agricultural growth (NACE A) declines by 1.93–7.36 percentage points in 99% of regions, whereas industry (NACE B–E) experiences smaller losses, with manufacturing (NACE C) emerging as relatively resilient. Our exercise indicates that ML models better capture nonlinear, seasonal, and spatial climate-economic interactions, highlighting the value of climate-augmented predictive modelling for early warning, regional fiscal planning, and targeted adaptation.
papers.reason: Quantifies sector-specific growth damages from European climate events using machine learning, offering useful inputs for regional fiscal and sector credit assessments.

papers.title: The consequences of optimism and pessimism for inflation dynamics and monetary policy
papers.abstract: We study how imperfect information about the persistence of economic fundamentals affects inflation dynamics and monetary policy. We focus on total factor productivity (TFP) growth, which encompasses demand- and supply-side effects linked to the post-COVID inflation surge. Agents in our model conduct Bayesian learning to infer the persistence of observed TFP growth rates. With imperfect information, waves of optimism and pessimism emerge, leading to a temporary divergence of inflation dynamics from fundamentals in terms of over- and undershooting. This mechanism helps explain the gradual rise of high inflation rates and the cautious monetary policy response in the aftermath of the COVID-19 crisis. Regarding optimal monetary policy, we find that a more hawkish stance is superior at reducing welfare losses and uncertainty arising in the imperfect-information model.
papers.reason: Models how imperfect information and TFP persistence generate inflation overshooting and argues for a more hawkish optimal monetary policy stance.

papers.title: On looking through sectoral shocks
papers.abstract: How does a possible de-anchoring of inflation expectations alter the conventional monetary policy prescription of look ing through sectoral shocks? To answer this question, we study optimal monetary policy in a multisector New Keyne sian model extended to allow for endogenous long-run inflation expectations. Wefindthattheriskofde-anchoringdoes not change the key policy trade-offs. It remains optimal for monetary policy to stabilise the output gap and inflation in sectors with stickier prices, confirming previous findings in the literature. Moreover, output and inflation dynamics are both hardly affected by a possible de-anchoring. This contrasts with the nominal interest rate response required to achieve these outcomes, which is more aggressive when there is a risk of de-anchoring. These findings reflect an asymmetry in the pass-through of inflation expectations to firms’ price-setting and households’ consumption decisions, with the latter being stronger than the former.
papers.reason: Analyzes optimal monetary policy in a multisector model with endogenous inflation expectations, showing that de-anchoring risks require a more aggressive nominal interest rate response.

papers.title: The 2025 U.S. tariffs on China and trade diversion to the EU
papers.abstract: We study whether bilateral trade barriers trigger trade diversion to third markets, using the 2025 increase in U.S. tariffs on Chinese goods and focusing on the European Union as an alternative destination. At the HS6 level, we construct a novel diversion-potential measure that combines realized U.S. tariff increases with product-level trade elasticities to predict the decline in Chinese exports to the United States. Trade diversion effects are limited to highly exposed products. Only products in the top decile of diversion potential experience a rise in export quantities to the EU. Unit values do not respond significantly.
papers.reason: Quantifies trade diversion effects to the EU from U.S. tariffs on China, offering clear implications for European trade and sectoral competitiveness.

papers.title: Learning monetary policy strategies at the effective lower bound with sudden surprises
papers.abstract: We examine how private sector agents might learn a new monetary strategy introduced while policy rates are at their effective lower bound (ELB) in an environment with large inflationary and deflationary shocks. We consider the adoption of a new asymmetric average inflation targeting rule aimed at countering the disinflationary bias imparted by the ELB. The most crucial time for learning runs from when rates would be near liftoff under the old strategy through early liftoff under the new rule. Recessionary shocks during this time could delay learning while large inflationary shocks could outright stop it, inhibiting the ability of the new strategy to address the costs associated with the ELB. Using the US post-Covid experience as an example, we also find that the monetary policy shocks can have important feedback on the learning process.
papers.reason: The study analyzes how private sector learning affects average inflation targeting at the effective lower bound using the US post-Covid experience, directly informing monetary policy and interest rate expectations.

papers.title: Strategic asset allocation with sustainability-linked bonds: A bivariate elasticity approach
papers.abstract: We study a continuous-time stochastic control problem in markets with state-dependent payoffs linked to a non-tradable performance variable, motivated by sustainability-linked bonds. The model features coupled tradable and non-tradable diffusion risks, generating endogenous return and volatility dynamics in an incomplete market. We introduce a bivariate elasticity transformation that reduces the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation to a quadratic control problem. This yields a closed-form log-utility portfolio policy and conditions describing how the non-tradable component affects portfolio risk through diversification or amplification.
papers.reason: The paper develops a quantitative portfolio choice framework for sustainability-linked bonds with direct relevance for asset allocators and green bond portfolio management.

papers.title: Mixing quantitative easing and interest rate policies at the effective lower bound: micro evidence from the euro area
papers.abstract: Abstract We study the interaction of expansionary rate-based monetary policy and quantitative easing, despite their concurrent implementation, by exploiting heterogeneous banks and the introduction of negative monetary-policy rates in a fragmented euro area. Quantitative easing increases credit supply less when banks’ funding costs do not decrease simultaneously. Using administrative data from Germany, we uncover that among banks selling their securities, central-bank reserves remain disproportionately with high-deposit banks that are constrained due to sticky customer deposits at the zero lower bound. Affected German banks lend relatively less to firms while increasing their interbank exposure in the euro area.
papers.reason: Directly informs the transmission mechanism of quantitative easing and negative interest rates to bank credit supply and interbank positioning in the euro area.

papers.title: Navigating climate policy shocks
papers.abstract: How should monetary policy respond to climate policy shocks? We develop an Environmental New-Keynesian model with green and fossil energy to assess the macroeconomic impacts of carbon pricing and green subsidy shocks and to identify the optimal monetary policy responses. Our findings indicate that these shocks create a policy trade-off between stabilizing inflation and the output gap. This trade-off is resolved in favor of output-gap stabilization, with optimal monetary policy focusing on dampening real output fluctuations while temporarily looking through inflation movements. Dual mandate Taylor rules yield lower welfare costs than inflation-only targeting rules and align the welfare performances of core and headline inflation targeting regimes.
papers.reason: Analyzes the optimal monetary policy response to carbon pricing and green subsidy shocks using a New-Keynesian model, directly informing central bank strategy and inflation targeting.

papers.title: Banks and nature
papers.abstract: Banks and nature: How strongly does the banking sector in Germany depend on ecosystem services? Banks and nature: How strongly does the banking sector in Germany depend on ecosystem services? Annette Becker, Marvin Dransfeld, Fabian Genswein, Emily Kormanyos, Paolo Krischak, Carina Schlam, Julia Thomas This study examines the dependency of the banking sector in Germany on ecosystem services through its corporate lending. Ecosystem services are derived from nature’s capacity to provide inputs for economic activity. We analyze how banks overall and categories of banks in Germany depend on ecosystem services, both directly and indirectly. Our findings indicate that banks are particularly reliant on a number of ecosystem services that relate either to water resources, or to water-regulating aspects. Additionally, indirect dependencies from supply chain connections frequently outweigh direct ones, and regionally focused banks show higher dependencies on ecosystem services compared to other categories of banks. These results underscore the importance of a better comprehension of nature-related risks and their implications for banks. Becker, A., M. Dransfeld, F. Genswein, E. Kormanyos, P. Krischak, C. Schlam, J. Thomas (2026), Banks and nature: How strongly does the banking sector in Germany depend on ecosystem services?, Technical Paper, No 03/2026.
papers.reason: Evaluates German banks' direct and indirect credit dependencies on ecosystem services, offering niche micro-level inputs for environmental risk assessment.

papers.title: Between Secrecy and Ostentation: Shrines and Rites for the Barbarous Relic
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Central bank gold vaults occupy a paradoxical position in contemporary monetary systems: They are among the most symbolically charged and institutionally significant spaces of modern finance, yet they have received almost no scholarly attention. This article argues that gold vaults cannot be understood solely as technical infrastructures for the safekeeping of bullion. Rather, they are hybrid spaces that oscillate between secrecy and ostentation, fortress and shrine, rational security apparatus and ritual site. Drawing on historical analysis, semiotics, and anthropological theories of value, I show how vaults materialize political imaginaries of sovereignty, embody cosmologies of value, and perform ritual functions that anchor collective belief in monetary order. The first part traces the evolution of vault architecture in France, the United Kingdom, Spain, and the United States, demonstrating how their militarization responded to shifting geopolitical and technological threats while simultaneously projecting state power. The second part examines the latent ritual and apotropaic dimensions of vaults in the post–Bretton Woods era, when gold's monetary role diminished even as its symbolic potency intensified. By foregrounding the dual nature of vaults as both defensive infrastructures and sacred repositories, the article reveals how these spaces help produce confidence, authenticate value, and sustain the mythic foundations of contemporary capitalism.
papers.reason: A qualitative study on the architectural, semiotic, and ritual dimensions of central bank gold vaults with no direct implications for financial markets.

papers.title: Seventy Years of Identifying the Phillips Curve and the Policy Rule
papers.abstract: Two coefficients enter nearly every quantitative argument about monetary policy: the Phillips-curve slope and the policy rule's response to inflation. For seventy years, each generation that estimated them identified the coefficient conditional on assumptions it maintained, and its successor relaxed one of them, naming the bias this exposed. This survey reconstructs the two programs as a single identification problem. It distinguishes five senses in which a coefficient has been called identified, reads each generation of the curve and of the rule in that key, and shows that the programs fail together because each borrows its identifying condition from the other. The same sequence ran on the latent inflation target and on the optimal rule. The survey closes on what the credible designs license when they leave a range rather than a point: bounds, signs and orderings, and decisions designed for a range.
papers.reason: Surveys seventy years of econometric identification challenges regarding the Phillips curve and monetary policy rules, offering methodological insights rather than direct market forecasts.

papers.title: Normalized Uncertainty: measures of uncertainty and directional risk from survey density forecasts
papers.abstract: Implementation of Normalized Uncertainty (NU, at the calibration a = b = 1 that needs no estimate), Normalized Growth Uncertainty (NGU) and Asymmetry Coherence (AC), measures that remove from survey forecast dispersion the part explained by the distance of expected inflation from the announced target and read directional risk where the asymmetry of a density is coherent with its central forecast, together with the scripts reproducing the public-data exhibits of the working papers 'Uncertain and Asymmetric Forecasts' and 'Tolerable Inflation, Intolerable Uncertainty' (Eric Vansteenberghe, Banque de France).
papers.reason: Introduces new quantitative measures to parse survey forecast dispersion and assess directional risk in inflation expectations.

papers.title: Tolerable Inflation, Intolerable Uncertainty
papers.abstract: Numerical inflation targets anchor beliefs. Across euro-area and US professional forecasts, inflation swaps and options, and realized inflation, uncertainty about inflation is compressed at the announced number and kinks exactly there. This paper identifies a cost of the same design that, to our knowledge, has not been shown before, and that appears in second moments only. Within the workhorse New Keynesian model, tolerating part of the inflation a supply shock produces is optimal, yet the optimal tolerated share is not identified: optimal look-through and an unwarranted drift of the effective target are observationally equivalent in the inflation history, so a central bank cannot demonstrate that a warranted deviation is warranted, ex post as much as in real time. Agents holding finite, heterogeneous patience then generate predictive variance that is flat below the target and rises linearly with the expected overshoot above it -- an observational-equivalence bill, zero at the announced number and accumulating with the point-years inflation spends above it. The first-order benefit of the number stands; what the cost changes is how inflation uncertainty must be measured. The distance from target explains 70% of the variation in professional forecast variance, and the bill lies within that component; Normalized Uncertainty -- to our knowledge the first such correction -- removes it. The purge changes inference substantially: on French loan-level data, raw dispersion is unrelated to corporate loan rates, while one standard deviation of the purged measure is associated with rates 89 basis points higher, and cross-country growth and time-series results shift similarly. Conventional measures of inflation uncertainty partly record inflation's distance from its anchor rather than uncertainty about the outlook.
papers.reason: The paper examines inflation targets, forecast dispersion, and second-moment uncertainty across euro-area and US markets, with implications for monetary policy credibility.

papers.title: Equilibrium prices under hidden Markov fundamentals
papers.abstract: We study a representative-agent Epstein-Zin economy with geometric dividends and a hidden finite-state Markov drift. We allow the price-dividend ratio to contain an additional positive, absolutely continuous valuation factor and, within the class $\mathfrak C$ defined below and under the regularity, admissibility, and positivity conditions of our main theorem, equilibrium forces this factor to be constant, yielding belief-Markovian prices. In the two-state case, under the stated positivity condition and strictly positive transition intensities, we prove existence, uniqueness, endpoint smoothness, interior analyticity, and uniform bounds for the positive solution of the pricing equation. For $0 0$, we derive belief-dependent stock volatility, a European option-pricing PDE, and a leading short-maturity conditional risk-neutral log-return skewness expansion.
papers.reason: Provides theoretical pricing derivations with limited direct application for macroeconomic forecasting or tactical market views.

papers.title: TFP persistence and monetary policy
papers.abstract: In this paper, by using several statistical tools, we provide evidence of an increase in the persistence of the U.S. total factor productivity. In a forward looking model, agents' optimal behavior depends on the autocorrelation structure of the exogenous shocks. Since many monetary models are driven by exogenous TFP shocks, we study the interaction between monetary policy and TFP persistence. Considering a New-Keynesian model, first, we analytically derive the interaction between the TFP persistence, monetary policy parameters, and output gap and inflation. Second, we show that TFP persistence affects the optimal behavior of the monetary policy. Preliminary and incomplete draft
papers.reason: By analyzing how US total factor productivity persistence alters New-Keynesian transmission and optimal policy rules, the study provides direct insights for rate strategists.

papers.title: The Response of Consumption to Interest Rates with Borrowing Constraints: An Analytical Approach
papers.abstract: I derive an explicit mapping from initial assets, income and the real interest rate to consumption for an income fluctuation problem with a borrowing constraint and CARA utility. I show that there exists a threshold of initial wealth over which the partial equilibrium consumption response to a permanent increase in the real interest rate is positive, consistent with recent empirical evidence. I further show that precautionary savings reinforce the possibility of crowding in and that the possibility of a positive response extends to a more standard CRRA utility whenever the elasticity of intertemporal substitution is strictly less than 1.
papers.reason: Derives analytical conditions under which higher real interest rates positively impact consumption via borrowing constraints and precautionary savings, informing macroeconomic modeling.
