papers.title: The Heterogeneous Impact of Short-Time Work: From Saved Jobs to Windfall Effects
papers.abstract: Abstract This paper investigates the adoption of short-time work (STW) by firms and their participating employees. We present a model showing that STW can preserve jobs in firms facing severe negative revenue shocks, but not in less affected firms, where hours are reduced without preventing layoffs. Using data from all French establishments during the 2008–2009 Great Recession, we find that STW helped save jobs and increased hours worked in firms hit by significant revenue losses, facilitating a faster post-recession recovery. We also identify substantial windfall effects, which raise the policy’s cost per job saved. Nonetheless, STW is likely more cost-effective at preserving employment than wage subsidies, potentially resulting in a net negative cost to public finances.
papers.reason: Using French firm-level data, the paper evaluates the employment and fiscal costs of short-time work policies during recessions.

papers.title: The Reaction of Financial Markets to the Releases of DeepSeek R1 and Kimi K3: A Critical Analysis
papers.abstract: This paper compares financial-market reactions to the releases of DeepSeek R1 in January 2025 and Kimi K3 in July 2026. Both AI models were presented as credible Chinese competitors near the capability frontier, but their releases conveyed different economic information. DeepSeek R1 combined open weights with unusually low reported training and inference costs, prompting investors to reassess expected demand for computing infrastructure and producing large stock-price decreases among semiconductor and data-centre-related firms. Kimi K3 instead entered at broadly frontier prices and generated a market reaction concentrated more heavily among rival Chinese AI laboratories. Drawing on descriptive event-window evidence, model capability and cost comparisons, subsequent industry developments, and the historical diffusion of open-source software, the paper argues that open-weight models redistribute rents across the AI value chain rather than eliminating them. Incumbents remain protected by complementary assets including distribution, product bundling, switching costs, proprietary data, serving capacity, and contractual trust. The analysis suggests that investors and policy makers should assess risks looking not only at model capability, but also at the ownership and durability of complementary assets across the AI value chain.
papers.reason: Examines financial market equity reactions to Chinese AI releases and analyzes how open-weight models redistribute rents across the tech value chain.

analysis.summary: This paper compares global equity market reactions to the releases of Chinese AI models DeepSeek R1 in January 2025 and Kimi K3 in July 2026. DeepSeek R1 combined open weights with low reported training costs, triggering sharp sell-offs in compute supply chain equities (NVIDIA -17.0%, SOX -9.1%) as investors marked down expected hardware demand. Conversely, Kimi K3 entered at near-frontier prices, concentrating losses among competing pure-play AI labs (Zhipu AI -35.1%, MiniMax -17.1%). The author argues open-weight models redistribute economic rents across the value chain rather than eliminating them, with incumbents shielded by complementary assets such as distribution, system integration, and trust.
key_takeaways: DeepSeek R1 (Jan 2025) drove hardware supply chain sell-offs (NVIDIA -17.0%, SOX -9.1%) by signaling low compute costs, while Kimi K3 (Jul 2026) primarily hit rival AI labs (Zhipu AI -35.1%).
OpenRouter total token usage surged from 0.53T to 58T per week between Jan 2025 and Jul 2026, while top US labs expanded absolute token volume nearly 40-fold (0.34T to 13.19T).

Incumbent AI providers preserve market power through complementary assets—including product bundling, switching costs, serving capacity, enterprise trust, and proprietary data moats—rather than raw model weights alone.

By demonstrating that open-weight model releases reallocate rents across the software stack rather than destroying aggregate tech value, the study helps quantify cross-sectional risks between chipmakers, specialized AI labs, and diversified tech incumbents. papers.title: A KAN-based Non-linear Factorization for Embedding Layer Compression
papers.abstract: Among existing embedding compression approaches, low-rank factorization provides a simple and mathematically principled solution by approximating the embedding matrix with a reduced-rank decomposition. However, its practical effectiveness is often limited, as the resulting linear bottleneck constrains representational capacity. To overcome these limitations, we propose an enhanced factorization scheme that increases expressive power by introducing learnable non-linear projections within the compressed embedding layer. Our method is inspired by the Kolmogorov Arnold Networks (KAN) paradigm, which replaces fixed linear transformations with learnable univariate functions. Despite promising results in other domains, applications of KANs in NLP remain scarce and have so far been largely limited to final or task specific layers, rather than core representational components such as embedding layers. We evaluate the proposed approach by integrating the compressed embedding layer into the Skip-gram framework and comparing it against a standard low-rank baseline under matched parameter budgets on the Word Analogy and Semantic Similarity benchmarks. We further introduce an effective initialization strategy from a pre-trained, uncompressed embedding layer. The behavior of the model is analyzed both immediately after initialization and after a brief post-initialization refinement phase, considering training with the standard Skip-gram objective as well as variants augmented with distillation from the original embedding layer. Overall, our results show that augmenting low-rank factorization with learnable non-linear projections effectively mitigates the limitations of linear bottlenecks, yielding more faithful compressed embeddings under fixed dimensionality and suggesting a promising direction for embedding layer compression beyond purely linear methods.
papers.reason: Pure computer science methodology focused on embedding layer compression via Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks, with no financial or macroeconomic application.

papers.title: JaxMARL-BC: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Macroeconomic Modelling, in Seconds
papers.abstract: Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) offers a principled way of populating simulated economies with many heterogeneous decision makers. Its adoption, pioneered in finance, has nonetheless been slow in macroeconomics because of two main limitations: the lack of a shared frame of reference connecting MARL systems to dynamic stochastic general equilibrium (DSGE) models the profession already trusts, and the very long training times. The first limitation was recently addressed by the Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Business Cycle (MARL-BC), which places deep RL households in a real business cycle economy and reduces to classic DSGE models in specific limits. Here we address the second limitation. We present JaxMARL-BC, a JAX-accelerated simulator that trains MARL-BC economies in seconds (between 75x and 724x faster than the reference implementation), and scales to 200,000 independent learning households. We verify its correctness against the known DSGE limits, characterise its scaling through a simple cost law, and demonstrate its value by a proof-of-concept calibration of an extended model with heterogeneous returns on capital, in a two-hour experiment that would previously have taken over a month. We release JaxMARL-BC as open source.
papers.reason: The paper provides a technical advancement in macroeconomic simulation methods using machine learning, offering faster estimation of DSGE models with indirect relevance for macro forecasters.

papers.title: National Wage Contracts, Monopsony, and Welfare in a North-South Economy,
papers.abstract: Abstract In countries characterized by significant geographical disparities in productivity, nationwide labour contracts may cause local unemployment by preventing the adjustments that would occur in a competitive labour market. Here we argue, however, that when there are mobility frictions and monopsony power, nationwide contracts may still be preferable to local contracts. Using a spatial general equilibrium model calibrated on the Italian North-South divide, we suggest that nationwide wage contracts may still lead to narrower regional welfare gaps if monopsony power is sufficiently strong in low-productivity areas.
papers.reason: The paper investigates the impact of nationwide wage contracts and monopsony power on regional employment and welfare using an Italian calibration.

papers.title: Replication package for: Investment-Goods Market Power and Capital Accumulation
papers.abstract: This page provides the replication package for the paper “Investment-Goods Market Power and Capital Accumulation” by Fabio Bertolotti, Andrea Lanteri, and Alessandro T. Villa. The ZIP archive contains all data and code required to replicate the results. The README.txt file provides a description of the files included in the package and instructions for running the code to reproduce the figures.

papers.title: Estimating the Macroeconomic Effects of Oil Supply News
papers.abstract: A common approach for estimating the macroeconomic effects of oil supply news employs SVAR-IV models identified using changes in oil futures prices around OPEC quota announcements as an instrument. However, we show that the reduced-form oil price innovations, structural shocks, and the instrumental variable in these estimations are all Granger-caused by financial variables, indicating informational deficiencies in the VAR model and contamination of the instrument. To resolve these issues, we incorporate financial indicators into the econometrician’s information set, yielding significantly different results. These include a sharper short-term output decline, lower and less persistent inflationary effects, and a reversal of the monetary policy response. Our results also show greater stability over time and the disappearance of puzzling responses. Finally, we identify similar issues in other prominent oil-market SVAR models, suggesting that informational deficiencies are a pervasive issue in oil-market research.
papers.reason: Demonstrates that omitting financial indicators in oil-market SVAR models biases estimates of output, inflation, and monetary policy responses to oil supply shocks.

papers.title: Globalization and Regional Divergence: Evidence from the Italian Provinces (1871–1911)
papers.abstract: Abstract This paper examines the regional economic impact of the First Globalization in Italy. We combine national-level trade data with provincial employment data for 35 tradable agricultural and manufacturing sectors to measure the trade exposure of Italian provinces to imports and exports. We then assess how changes in trade exposure (trade shocks) are related to employment growth across provinces. Our results show that the South was consistently more negatively affected by trade shocks than the North. We also show that, similarly to employment growth, international migration was influenced by agricultural import shocks, with the South experiencing a stronger migration response compared to the North. In contrast to employment growth, gross domestic product (GDP) per worker growth did not exhibit a sizable differential impact of any trade shock between the North and the South.
papers.reason: Analyzes the historical regional impact of trade exposure across Italian provinces from 1871 to 1911, offering limited direct implications for modern financial markets.

papers.abstract: This is the replication package for "Beliefs and the Incentive Effects of Preferential College Admissions: Evidence from an Experiment and a Structural Model", accepted in 2026 by the Journal of Political Economy.

papers.title: Relaxed Sender Anonymity for CBDC Interbank Settlement: A Zero-Knowledge Approach on Permissioned EVM
papers.abstract: Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC) interbank settlement systems operating on Distributed Ledger Technology (DLT) face a fundamental trade-off: blockchain transparency enables trustless verification but exposes commercially sensitive bilateral transaction flows to all network participants. We propose a confidential interbank settlement protocol for permissioned Ethereum-compatible networks that resolves this tension through a relaxed sender anonymity model tailored to regulatory AML/CFT requirements. In this model, the initiating institution remains publicly identifiable on-chain for accountability and compliance, while the receiving institution, transfer amount, and business payload are cryptographically obfuscated. We realize the protocol on Hyperledger Besu using QBFT consensus, combining Groth16 zero-knowledge proofs over BN254, Poseidon hash commitments in an incremental Merkle tree, multi-recipient ECIES payload encryption, and an on-chain NoteRegistry contract that stores encrypted notes as an append-only ledger log, eliminating trusted off-chain custody servers. The protocol supports shield, confidential transfer, and unshield state transitions. Experimental evaluation across a five-node network (three commercial banks, a central bank operator, and a securities depository) demonstrates end-to-end settlement in 8-16 s, proof verification overhead of about 1 ms (around 220k gas) via EVM precompiles, and client proof generation in 4-12 s on commodity ARM hardware. While receiver confidentiality is established at the protocol level, the current proof-of-concept NoteRegistry uses owner-indexed events, a trade-off addressable in production via uniform event broadcasting.
papers.reason: It proposes and tests a concrete cryptographic architecture for confidential CBDC interbank settlement on DLT, directly informing bank digital asset strategy and payment market infrastructure.

papers.title: Thresholding Post-Quantum Signatures
papers.abstract: Threshold signature schemes distribute the signing process among $T$ parties out of $N$. They enable a variety of applications and their research is also motivated by a recent NIST call. However, applications are dominated by pre-quantum signatures, which are more efficient but not secure in the post-quantum setting. This paper investigates existing post-quantum signatures, based on a variety of paradigms: lattice problems, one-way (hash) functions, cryptographic group actions, isogenies and multivariate systems. We propose a classification (divided by paradigm) of existing tools that are used to build $T$-out-of-$N$ schemes from digital signatures. We also include general approaches based on FHE, MPC or ZKP.
papers.reason: The study classifies post-quantum threshold signature schemes for DLT, offering technical insights for blockchain security but no direct macroeconomic or asset-pricing conclusions.

papers.title: Managing geopolitical risk in banking systems: an integrative framework based on a systematic and bibliometric review
papers.abstract: Purpose This study examines how geopolitical risk (GPR) affects the banking sector by influencing financial stability, bank behaviour, risk exposure and organisational decision-making. Evidence remains fragmented across banking, finance and management studies, and this review addresses the gap by synthesising how geopolitical shocks are transmitted to banks and how financial institutions respond through governance, risk management and strategic adaptation. Design/methodology/approach A PRISMA-inspired systematic literature review of 58 peer-reviewed articles (2000–2026) was conducted using Scopus and Google Scholar, with bibliometric profiling, structured content analysis and thematic synthesis. Findings GPR affects banks through financial, institutional, economic and behavioural channels, increasing credit risk, market volatility, capital allocation constraints and systemic fragility. Bank responses depend on governance quality, capital strength and strategic flexibility, while managerial mechanisms and organisational adaptation processes remain underexplored. Research limitations/implications The framework is inductive and requires empirical validation. Evidence on micro-level managerial responses remains scarce, with only three studies addressing organisational adaptation at the firm level. Practical implications The findings support bank executives, regulators and policymakers in embedding GPR indicators into enterprise risk management, scenario-based stress testing and governance frameworks. Originality/value The study advances the GPR literature by developing a multi-level integrative framework that makes the firm-to-bank transmission channel explicit, incorporates four bank risk categories (credit, market, liquidity/funding and operational/cyber) and identifies governance quality and institutional capacity as key moderating mechanisms, a conceptual structure absent from prior narrative reviews in this domain.
papers.reason: A literature review examining how geopolitical risk affects bank stability and credit risk, offering general frameworks rather than direct econometric asset-pricing estimates.

papers.title: Replication package for "National Wage Contracts, Monopsony, and Welfare in a North-South Economy"
papers.abstract: This package contains the data, programs and instructions to replicate manuscript “National Wage Contracts, Monopsony, and Welfare in a North-South Economy" by E. Ciani, A. Dalmazzo and G. de Blasio, forthcoming at JEEA.

papers.title: Macroprudential regulation: A risk management approach
papers.abstract: We develop a credit-risk based framework for macroprudential policy that treats systemic risk as the credit exposure of a policymaker to a portfolio of supervised banks. Using a structural credit model estimated from Credit Default Swap (CDS) prices, we derive the socially optimal capital buffers per bank by balancing the benefits of lower systemic risk against the economic costs of higher capital requirements through reduced credit supply. Applying this framework to Europe’s systemic banks, we find that the market-based optimal buffers are substantially higher than those currently in use and vary significantly across institutions. Conditional on current country averages, within-country buffers are aligned close to optimally; suboptimality mostly arises from substantial differences between country averages.
papers.reason: Derives market-based optimal capital buffers for European systemic banks using CDS data, providing direct implications for bank capital requirements, credit supply, and financial stability.

papers.title: Post burn contracture neck: Experience in government medical college, Srinagar
papers.abstract: Background and Aim: Post-burn neck contracture is one of the most debilitating complications of burn injuries, resulting in significant functional limitation, cosmetic deformity, and psychological distress. The burden of post-burn contractures remains high in developing countries due to delayed presentation, inadequate primary burn care, and poor access to reconstructive services. Kashmir Valley, with its prolonged winters and widespread use of traditional heating devices, experiences a considerable number of thermal burn injuries requiring reconstructive intervention. This study was undertaken to evaluate the clinical profile, surgical management, and early functional outcomes of patients with post-burn neck contractures treated at Government Medical College, Srinagar. Methods: A prospective observational study was conducted in the Department of Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery, Government Medical College, Srinagar, over a period of 26 months from March 2024 to April 2026. A total of 40 patients with post-burn neck contracture were included irrespective of age and gender. Detailed demographic and clinical data were recorded. Patients underwent contracture release followed by split-thickness skin grafting, Z-plasty, or local flap reconstruction based on the severity of contracture and scar characteristics. Postoperative outcomes, complications, cervical range of motion, and recurrence were assessed during follow-up. Data were analysed using SPSS version 26 and expressed as frequencies, percentages, mean ± standard deviation, and appropriate statistical tests. Results: Among the 40 patients, the majority belonged to the 21–40-year age group (47.5%), with males accounting for 57.5% of the study population. Flame burns were the most common etiology (52.5%), followed by Kangri burns (25%). Moderate neck contracture was the most frequent clinical presentation (47.5%). Contracture release with split-thickness skin grafting was the most commonly performed procedure (47.5%), followed by local flap reconstruction (35%) and Z-plasty (17.5%). Complete graft or flap survival was achieved in 90% of patients. Satisfactory improvement in cervical range of motion was observed in 92.5% of patients, while postoperative recurrence occurred in only 2.5% during the follow-up period. Conclusions: Post-burn neck contracture continues to be a significant reconstructive challenge in Kashmir Valley. Split-thickness skin grafting remains the most frequently performed surgical procedure with satisfactory early functional outcomes. Careful patient selection, meticulous surgical planning, appropriate reconstructive techniques, postoperative splintage, and supervised physiotherapy play a crucial role in minimizing complications and recurrence. Long-term multicentric studies are recommended to further evaluate the durability of different reconstructive techniques.
papers.reason: A clinical study on post-burn neck contracture surgery with no relevance to economic or financial markets.

papers.title: Fiscal Policy and the Saving Glut of the Rich
papers.abstract: Since the 1980s, the United States has experienced a pronounced saving glut of the rich, a large accumulation of assets among the top 1% of earners.We argue that this development partly reflects a shift in the financing of redistributive policies, from inflationary finance in the 1960s and 1970s to debt finance backed by future taxation beginning in the early 1980s.The central insight is that, in the presence of a progressive tax system, a switch from inflationary to debt financing leads to debt accumulation by top earners.We develop a New Keynesian model with borrowers and savers in which redistributive transfers can be either funded or unfunded.Unfunded transfers generate fiscal inflation that erodes the real value of public and private debt, redistributing wealth through asset revaluation effects.Funded transfers, by contrast, are financed through future taxes borne primarily by high-income households, which respond by accumulating claims on both households and the government.Using a structurally estimated version of the model, we find that the shift from unfunded to funded redistribution in the 1980s contributed significantly to the subsequent saving glut of the rich.
papers.reason: Connects the shift from inflationary finance to debt-financed redistributive policies in the US to the accumulation of assets among top earners.

papers.title: The Taming of the Skew: Asymmetric Inflation Risk and Monetary Policy
papers.abstract: Time-varying asymmetric inflation risks generate persistent stagflationary effects. A quantitative general equilibrium model with time-varying skewness in the distribution of cost-push shocks matches these effects. Central to the analysis is a representation theorem that provides a tractable characterization of a broad class of models with asymmetric shock distributions. The theorem enables a closed-form characterization of optimal monetary policy, according to which the central bank should lean against the balance of inflation risks, while rendering quantitative general-equilibrium models with time-varying risks amenable to counterfactual and scenario analysis.
papers.reason: Provides a closed-form framework for optimal monetary policy under asymmetric inflation risks, directly informing interest rate policy and stagflation scenarios.

papers.title: Oil Prices and Global Activity in a General Equilibrium Model with Dynamic Elasticities
papers.abstract: This paper develops a dynamic general equilibrium model of the global crude oil market that delivers horizon-dependent price elasticities of oil supply and demand, arising from the gradual adjustment of oil producers and consumers over time. We refer to elasticities beyond the impact horizon as dynamic elasticities. We derive closed-form expressions for the elasticities, which allow us to impose transparent prior restrictions in the empirical analysis and to quantify how dynamic elasticities shape the propagation of structural shocks to oil prices and global real activity. We estimate the model with Bayesian methods using monthly data on industrial production and key oil-market indicators — production, inventories, and prices. Diffuse priors on dynamic elasticities imply elasticity profiles that are essentially flat across horizons. By contrast, informative priors — or an expanded information set including drilling activity under diffuse elasticity priors — yield elasticities that rise with the horizon, increase the contribution of supply shocks to fluctuations in oil prices and real activity, and reduce that of oil-consumption demand shocks.
papers.reason: Provides a macroeconomic framework for evaluating oil supply and demand elasticities, relevant for commodity analysts and inflation forecasters.

papers.title: Capital-Skill Complementarity Beyond Firm Boundaries
papers.abstract: New machinery has long been argued to raise the relative demand for skilled labor, yet firm-level evidence finds no such shift at investing firms. We resolve this puzzle by looking beyond firm boundaries. Linking Belgian data on capital investments, buyer–supplier transactions, and worker skills, we show that the skill bias of new machinery arises entirely at external suppliers. Following machinery investment spikes, purchases from suppliers raise firms’ total demand for high-STEM workers by 45%, three times the rise for other skill groups, while in-house hiring raises it by less than 5%, evenly across skill groups. This external demand comes first from machine integrators and later from complementary services such as software, and is stronger for smaller firms, lumpier investments, and rapidly advancing capital, consistent with fixed and adjustment costs of hiring high-STEM workers in-house. In a general-equilibrium model estimated on our event studies, the rise in machinery per worker from 2003 to 2021 raises relative demand for high-STEM workers by 8.8 log points and their wage premium by 3.1. Measured on payrolls alone, both would fall.
papers.reason: Examines how capital investments shift labor demand to external suppliers using Belgian firm-level data, offering indirect insights for structural wage dynamics.

papers.title: Ratcheting up Paris
papers.abstract: The Paris Agreement is designed to increase climate ambition gradually through a process of ratcheting up. What is the plausible endpoint of this process? To answer this question, we develop a tractable integrated assessment model in which countries interact through a decentralized general equilibrium and negotiate unanimously over a global carbon budget, with all mitigation implemented via a global carbon price. We prove the existence and uniqueness of a unanimous international agreement on global emissions, in which carbon pricing revenues are redistributed across countries in proportion to marginal climate damages. In a quantitative application for 154 countries, the resulting equilibrium limits global mean surface temperature change to 1.51°C, at a carbon price of 320 USD/tCO 2 . The associated international transfers of carbon pricing revenue are progressive toward lower-income countries and amount to about 0.8% of global GDP annually - an order of magnitude larger than the Paris Agreement’s climate finance target.
papers.reason: Provides a global quantitative assessment of an international carbon pricing and revenue redistribution agreement.

papers.title: Rethinking Official Statistics Beyond Averages: Centering Lived Experience
papers.abstract: Official statistics face a fundamental paradox: data has never been more abundant, yet public trust in the institutions that produce it has never felt more precarious. This paper argues that the crisis is not primarily one of methodological failure or statistical illiteracy, but of representational legitimacy: aggregate indicators systematically fail to capture lived experience, and citizens increasingly do not recognize themselves in the numbers that purport to describe them. We situate this argument within a broader body of work on moving “from averages to agency”. We place lived experience at the analytical center, drawing on three intellectual traditions that official statistics has engaged less systematically: the mixed methods tradition in social research, the citizen science movement as recently codified in the Copenhagen Framework on Citizen Data, and the participation literature descending from Arnstein's ladder. Drawing on emerging practices from statistical agencies across more than a dozen countries, we take stock of pathways through which official statistics are beginning to shift from passive measurement toward active participation. Because participation is not a single practice but a family of practices, we propose a matrix of engagement that crosses depth of participation with the stages of the data value chain, arguing for fit-for-purpose rather than maximal participation. We conclude with a research agenda organized around methodological integration, scalability, the ethics of social licence, and institutional transformation.
papers.reason: Discusses methodological approaches to official statistics and public trust without direct bearing on financial markets or macroeconomic forecasting.

papers.title: Deregulation and Investment Spillovers in Multi-Product Production Settings
papers.abstract: This paper studies how the removal of price regulation was associated with changes in quality, efficiency, and welfare in the Belgian bread and cake industry. In the summer of 2004, price controls on bread were abolished. Because most firms in this industry produce both bread and cakes, the reform provides a useful setting in which to examine both direct changes in the deregulated market and spillovers to a related product line. We use detailed firm-product-level information on values and physical quantities to estimate product quality, technical efficiency, marginal costs, markups, and welfare. We find that deregulation was associated with substantial improvements in both quality and efficiency. Welfare increased through gains in consumer surplus and producer surplus, and the gains were not confined to bread. We also find evidence of spillovers to cake production, suggesting that deregulation encouraged technological upgrading that affected firms' broader production process.
papers.reason: The paper provides a firm-level microeconomic study of price deregulation in the Belgian bread and cake industry with only indirect implications for broader macroeconomic or market trends.
