Complete records of each firm’s AI use, linked to its monthly operations and sales, let us trace adoption through changes in business capabilities, such as reaching customers and introducing new products, to sales growth. Using a matched difference-in-differences design and focusing on firms with annual sales below RMB 5 million, we find that adoption raises monthly sales by 51.6%, primarily through a 47.0% increase in the number of orders; instrumental-variable estimates confirm these results. Adopters reach more customers, update their product lines faster, and deliver better product and service quality, with the largest proportional gains for the smallest firms. Two mechanisms help explain the results. First, AI lowers the cost of routine work: adopters produce more product content and change listings more often while spending less staff time per order, and the gains are largest for firms that faced the highest costs relative to sales before adoption. Second, AI reduces information frictions: adopters post richer product information, and the gains are largest in markets where demand is hard to predict and matching quality is poor, especially for small firms. At the market level, product categories with greater pre-existing information frictions see more sales by existing firms, more entry, and more new products. AI expands markets rather than merely shifting sales from non-adopters to adopters.
papers.reason: Provides microeconomic evidence on firm growth and sales impacts from generative AI adoption in China, relevant to the broader corporate and tech sector outlook.

papers.title: The Main Monetary Policy Shock
papers.abstract: We propose a novel procedure to identify a main monetary policy (MMP) shock as the linear combination of monetary policy surprises that best explains macroeconomic fluctuations. Implemented with two standard high-frequency yield-curve surprises and the Boehm and Kroner (2024) non-yield shock, the MMP shock explains nontrivial business-cycle variation over the last 30 years, in contrast with prior findings. Moreover, the MMP shock differs markedly from a textbook monetary policy shock: a contractionary shock leaves interest rates mostly unchanged but persistently lowers headline prices and appreciates the dollar, while temporarily tightening financial conditions and depressing industrial production.
papers.reason: Directly informs monetary policy transmission, asset pricing, and FX strategists by proposing a new high-frequency identification of monetary policy shocks.

papers.title: Policy Evaluation Beyond Significance Testing: Evidence from Chicago's ShotSpotter Contract
papers.abstract: Program impact estimates that are not statistically significant are often treated as providing little guidance for policy choice, even when economically important effects remain plausible. In such cases, the decision-relevant task is not simply to test whether the effect differs from zero, but to estimate the probability distribution of programmatic effects. The importance of going beyond hypothesis testing is especially clear when evaluations are underpowered relative to the effect needed for benefits to exceed costs. We illustrate this point using Chicago’s contract for ShotSpotter, an acoustical gunshot detection system that reduces police response times and may therefore have improved survival among shooting victims. Using a geographic RD design, we estimate that ShotSpotter reduced the shooting fatality rate by 2.5 percentage points, equivalent to roughly 49 fewer deaths per year. Although the estimate is not statistically significant, its implied benefit far exceeds the cost of the service. To have enough statistical power under the hypothesis testing approach to detect an effect of this size would require 87 years’ worth of Chicago shooting data. We instead implement a decision-relevant perspective using Bayesian analysis, treating the life-saving effect as a random variable. We find positive expected net benefits, with posterior probabilities that benefits exceed costs ranging from 70% under a flat prior and a $0.5 million value of statistical life to 99.6% under a no-harm prior and a $13.6 million value. The results illustrate how reliance on statistical significance can discard decision-relevant evidence when economically meaningful effects are difficult to detect precisely.
papers.reason: Evaluates a local municipal policing contract with no direct implications for macroeconomics or financial markets.

papers.title: Who's Moving In? The Changing Age Composition of Migration to the Carolinas
papers.abstract: The Carolinas are attracting movers at various life stages, from students and professionals building careers in major metros like Charlotte and Raleigh, North Carolina, and Greenville, South Carolina, to retirees seeking coastal and mountain living. But over the last decade, the age profile of these movers has changed: Adults ages 55 and older now make up a noticeably larger share of migrants. This shift in age composition is not uniform, however. Counties differ widely in the direction and magnitude of these shifts. The scale of migration to the Carolinas makes these shifts consequential. Since 2021, the Carolinas have ranked in the top 5 states for net domestic migration. North Carolina has brought in over 80,000 domestic migrants, and South Carolina has brought in over 60,000 domestic migrants. With migration at this scale, even modest changes in age composition can have an outsized impact on communities. This analysis examines how the age composition of migrants has changed across counties, where those changes coincide with fast migration growth, and what that might mean for local communities.
papers.reason: Documents demographic shifts in domestic migration to the Carolinas, offering localized insights with modest macro-financial implications.

papers.title: A Common Pattern behind Diverging Fortunes: U.S. Tariffs and Exports from Canada and Mexico
papers.abstract: The 2025 U.S. tariff increases were followed by sharply different export outcomes in Canada and Mexico. Comparing the 12 months ending in April 2026 with calendar year 2024, Canadian goods exports to the United States fell about 10 percent, while Mexican exports rose about 16 percent, even though Mexico faced a higher average tariff exposure (figure 1). Do these contrasting outcomes mean that tariffs mattered for Canada but had little effect on Mexico, even though both economies depend heavily on the U.S. market?
papers.reason: Provides empirical evidence on the divergent export responses of Canada and Mexico following US tariff increases, offering direct implications for trade flows and regional FX.

papers.title: Gold Reserve Relocations: Are They Always Bad News for U.S. Dollar Reserves?
papers.abstract: This note reviews several publicized gold reserve relocations by central banks in the Netherlands, France, and Germany since 2013 and any concurrent changes in their U.S. dollar reserve allocations. Generally, the choice of where to custody gold reserves may in part reflect the perceived risk of sanctions or expropriation in the jurisdiction of custody alongside other considerations like the proximity to international gold markets.
papers.reason: Examines gold reserve relocations by European central banks and their relation to sanctions risks and US dollar reserve allocations.

papers.title: U.S. Private Credit Vehicles: Institutional Structure and Aggregate Balance Sheets
papers.abstract: The expansion of private credit has become one of the most significant developments in financial markets over the past decade. Yet, estimates of the size of the market vary considerably, in part because the term private credit is used to describe different instruments, investment strategies, and financial intermediaries.
papers.reason: Addresses the institutional structure and balance sheets of US private credit vehicles, a rapidly expanding segment of corporate credit markets.

papers.title: The Effect of Oil Prices on Core Inflation: Recent Evidence from the Advanced Economies
papers.abstract: Elevated oil prices and heightened geopolitical uncertainty have renewed interest in a longstanding policy question: do supply shocks like oil-price increases pose a transitory or a persistent threat to price stability? This note sheds light on this question by providing new evidence on whether the inflation process has changed.
papers.reason: Analyzes whether oil price shocks pose a persistent threat to core inflation across advanced economies, directly informing monetary policy and rates outlooks.

papers.title: Reserve Currencies and Stablecoins
papers.abstract: Reserve Currencies and Stablecoins Beth M. Hammack President and Chief Executive Officer Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland The SNB and Its Watchers Conference 2026 Panel Discussion, Stable Coins and the Demand and Price (Exchange Rate) of “Safe Hav en’’ Currencies UBS Konferenzzentrum Grünenhof Zürich, Switzerland November 5, 2026 For release on delivery 8:50 am EST November 5, 2026 1 Introduction Thank you to the Karl Brunner Institute of Macroeconomic Policy for the kind invitation to speak at the SNB and Its Watchers conference this year. I look forward to a great discussion with Hans, Thomas, and Carolyn. And thank you to Gianluca for moderating. The role of safe haven currencies in our world economy is always an important topic of discussion. I previously spoke on this in March at the University of Chicago Booth School of Business’s US Monetary Policy Forum.1 Today’s panel—with its focus on stablecoins—provides an intriguing angle through which to discuss evolving dynamics of safe-haven currencies. First, I’ll note that the views I express today are mine and not those of the Federal Reserve System or my colleagues on the Federal Open Market Committee. Why the Dollar Stands Apart The dollar’s position as the world’s reserve currency depends first and foremost on the United States’ strong rule of law. Our legal institutions provide a reliable framework for enforcing contracts and protecting property rights.
papers.reason: Discusses the evolution of safe-haven currencies and the intersection with stablecoin adoption, carrying broad implications for global FX and capital flows.

papers.title: Reciprocal Deposits: An Update
papers.abstract: Reciprocal deposits are deposits exchanged between banks to increase deposit insurance coverage for a depositor. The recently-passed 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act significantly increased the quantity of reciprocal deposits that are not counted as brokered deposits. This Economic Commentary describes the change, how this change increases the deposit insurance limit in practice, and which banks are likely to increase their use of reciprocal deposits as a consequence.
papers.reason: Provides a useful institutional update on reciprocal deposits and bank funding conditions under recent US legislation, with limited broader macro impact.

papers.title: The Information Effect, Policy Rule Ambiguity, and the Decomposition of Monetary Policy Surprises
papers.abstract: I study a New Keynesian economy in which the private sector has imperfect information about both the underlying shock and the monetary policy rule. The information effect of monetary policy makes the two sources of imperfect information interact with each other. On the normative side, I show that the conventional certainty equivalence result regarding optimal monetary policy breaks down. The optimal policy rule becomes less responsive to the underlying shock, and depends on the degree of rule ambiguity. On the positive side, in a dynamic New Keynesian model calibrated to the US economy, I decompose monetary policy surprises into shock uncertainty, rule ambiguity, and the interaction effect. I find that the interaction effect accounts for more than 70 percent of the variance of monetary policy surprises.
papers.reason: Decomposes US monetary policy surprises through the lens of rule ambiguity and information effects, offering direct relevance for rates and macro strategists.

papers.title: Minimum Wage, Business Dynamism, and the Life Cycle of Firms
papers.abstract: This paper studies the effects of the minimum wage on the life cycle of firms. We start by building a tractable model where heterogeneous firms have labor market power, invest in innovation, and choose formal or informal sectors. The model predicts that a minimum wage hike not only shrinks the young and lower-productivity firms but also decreases the incentives to innovate, resulting in slower life-cycle growth. We show that these predictions hold in Brazilian administrative and census data, leveraging the variation in exposure to the minimum wage between 1999 and 2010. An increase in the minimum wage (i) decreases the growth rates of small and young establishments and (ii) increases the growth rates of old and large establishments. At the municipal level, we observe an increase in informal employment and in the earnings of both formal and informal workers. Lastly, we augment our simple model into a full quantitative general equilibrium model with monopsonistic firms, endogenous innovation, and formal-informal choice, calibrated to the Brazilian economy. A counterfactual minimum wage increase generates reallocation from young to old firms, dampens innovation at low-productivity firms, and expands the informal sector. Our findings suggest that the minimum wage is a possible explanation for the decline in the importance of young establishments and business dynamism in Brazil.
papers.reason: Examines the impact of minimum wages on firm life cycles and informality using Brazilian data, offering clear structural insights for emerging market economies.

papers.title: Labor Market Tightness and Minority Earnings Gaps
papers.abstract: We study how labor-market tightness affects minority earnings gaps using administrative data for US metropolitan areas from 2010 to 2025. After accounting for national shocks, local seasonality, and local trends, a 1-percentage-point unemployment decline reduces the white-minus-minority earnings gap by about 0.2 percentage points for all jobs and 0.3 percentage points for new stable hires. These responses strengthen as slack declines, reaching 0.4 and 0.6 percentage points, respectively, in hot markets. Neither observed worker and vacancy composition nor concurrent policy changes account for these effects. Increased mobility and upgrading across broad job categories explain little of the narrowing, although hiring distributions become more similar between the two groups. Where recruiting is concentrated among fewer employers, the earnings-gap response varies less with slack. Together, the findings point toward relative earnings improvements within labor-market segments and employer competition as a mechanism through which tightness narrows minority earnings gaps.
papers.reason: Documents the relationship between labor market tightness and minority earnings gaps across US metropolitan areas, contributing to ongoing employment and wage assessments.

papers.title: Innovation in the relationships between central banks and central counterparties
papers.abstract: Remarks delivered by Sam Schulhofer-Wohl at the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago Financial Markets Group Fall Conference.
papers.reason: The title addresses a global institutional relationship without specifying a geographic market.

papers.title: Inequality, Risk, and Business Cycles
papers.abstract: We quantify the connection between inequality, risk, and business cycles in a medium-scale New Keynesian model with tractable household heterogeneity, estimated with aggregate and cross-sectional data. We find that inequality and risk substantially amplify cyclical fluctuations. Most of this amplification operates through cyclical precautionary saving induced by countercyclical idiosyncratic risk. Savers reduce their consumption to insure themselves against large income drops, whose likelihood rises in recessions. Independent evidence supports both the magnitude and broad incidence of this recessionary increase in risk across skill and income groups, and indicates that the sizable, countercyclical premium on illiquid claims generated by the same mechanism is quantitatively plausible.
papers.reason: Quantifies how household heterogeneity and precautionary savings amplify macroeconomic fluctuations, informing models of business cycles and asset pricing.

papers.title: Tax Productivity and Economic Development: A Quantitative Macroeconomic Analysis
papers.abstract: This paper examines the role of government capacity to collect taxes in driving economic development. We first draw on a new macro-historical database to document that tax collections relative to tax administration expenditures rise sharply with GDP per capita. We then interpret this finding in a neoclassical growth model with a tax administration sector in which labor inputs are required to raise tax revenues. Countries differ in their levels of tax productivity, capturing how effectively labor is used to raise taxes, as well as their levels of productivity in creating consumption and investment goods. Governments use tax revenues to provide public capital that complements private factors in production and to make transfers. Quantitatively, our model predicts that increases in tax productivity in low-income economies can raise GDP per capita substantially more than suggested by Hulten’s theorem.
papers.reason: Analyzes the link between tax administration capacity and economic development in a growth model, providing solid long-run structural analysis with indirect market relevance.

papers.title: Has U.S. Monetary Policy Really Improved? A 150‑Year Perspective
papers.abstract: Has U.S. monetary policy actually improved over time? Or was the apparent success of the modern Federal Reserve mostly the result of more favorable economic conditions and better luck? In this post, we summarize our paper,* which develops a framework for comparing monetary policy across different economic environments. Our approach asks how close policy came to the best response given the economic conditions and shocks policymakers faced. Applying this framework to 150 years of U.S. monetary history, we find that meaningful improvements in monetary policy occurred only in the last thirty years. Most of the gains reflect, among other developments, substantially better responses to financial shocks and supply shocks.
papers.reason: Evaluates 150 years of US monetary history and finds structural improvements in policy responses to financial and supply shocks over the last three decades.

papers.title: Dynamic Individuals, Static Neighborhoods: Migration and Earnings Changes in Poor Neighborhoods
papers.abstract: Why do poor neighborhoods stay poor? Using administrative data linking residential histories to longitudinal earnings, we show that while many residents of poor neighborhoods have persistently low earnings and remain in concentrated poverty for extended periods, a large number also experience sizable earnings growth and move to richer areas. Estimates based on idiosyncratic, firm-specific pay changes show that part of this sorting is causal — earnings increases induce upward moves. On net, selective migration depresses the growth of poor neighborhoods’ average earnings by roughly 60 percent and represents an underappreciated driver of the persistence of concentrated poverty.
papers.reason: Studies the micro-level link between earnings growth and residential migration in poor neighborhoods, with only indirect implications for aggregate labor market trends.

papers.title: Social Insurance with Imperfect Eligibility Screening: Theory and Evidence from Pandemic UI
papers.abstract: This paper studies social insurance with imperfect eligibility screening, focusing on unemployment insurance (UI) during its expansion in 2020 and 2021. We study the extent of imperfect screening by identifying anomalous payments using administrative tax data and UI policies, finding $214 billion in potentially-improper payments—concentrated in the Pandemic Unemployment Assistance (PUA) program—with approximately half detectable ex-ante through improved federal-state data sharing. There is substantial geographic variation, and a border design shows this is partly due to policy decisions made by states. To assess the implications for optimal policy, we first conduct simulations that replace PUA with means-tested, lump-sum transfers, finding that these transfers would have better insured against income losses at lower administrative cost. Second, we develop a model of opt-in versus automatic transfers that shows the targeting advantage of opt-in programs can reverse when ineligible recipients pass the benefit screen. Calibrated to 2020 UI, the model implies that shifting toward automatic transfers would have increased social welfare.
papers.reason: Examines eligibility screening and improper payments in US pandemic unemployment insurance, offering fiscal and administrative insights with limited immediate market relevance.

papers.title: US monetary policy, macroeconomic news and the global secular decline of interest rates
papers.abstract: The global secular decline in long-term interest rates since the 1990s has been largely driven by cumulative yield changes during U.S. monetary policy announcement windows (FOMC windows). We document this FOMC-window effect for a group of ten major advanced economies. Based on a term structure model, we show that the effect operates through the expected path of future short-term interest rates rather than term premia. We further find that the global secular decline in interest rates has been concentrated in FOMC windows preceded by macroeconomic news. We interpret this pattern as a “Fed response to news” channel and provide empirical evidence to support this interpretation. Keywords: Monetary policy, bond yields, interest rate trends, global financial cycle. We also thank Dongkeun Choi for excellent research assistance. All errors are ours. The views expressed in this paper are those of the authors and not necessarily the views of the BIS. papers.reason: It directly examines how US monetary policy announcements drive the global decline in long-term interest rates across advanced economies.
